### Decorative Book Binding

This image illustrates a historical book cover, likely fashioned from <term>pigskin or vellum<note>Vellum is a high-quality parchment made from calfskin, while pigskin was a durable alternative frequently used for heavy volumes.</note></term> stretched over wooden boards. 

The surface is decorated using a technique known as **<term>blind-tooling</term>** <note>A method where decorative patterns are impressed into the leather using heated metal tools without the application of gold leaf or color.</note>. The design is composed of several nested rectangular frames:

*   **Outer Frames:** These contain a repeating "roll" pattern. Within these borders are circular <term>medallions</term> <note>Small, circular portrait busts often used as decorative motifs.</note> depicting notable figures. These portraits are separated by ornate, flowing patterns of leaves and flowers.
*   **Central Panel:** The middle of the cover is divided into three vertical sections. The left and right sections are filled with vertical strips of Renaissance-style floral ornaments. The very center consists of four simple vertical lines pressed into the material.
*   **Bottom Inscription:** At the bottom center of the design, a specific medallion is visible, showing a figure in profile.

The only legible inscription within these decorative elements is:

<unclear>Erasmus</unclear> <note>original Latin: "ERASMVS." This refers to Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (c. 1466–1536), the celebrated Dutch humanist and scholar whose works were central to the intellectual life of the Renaissance.</note>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory epistle, transitioning from general theological disputes to the specific dangers of superstitions regarding witchcraft. Catchword from previous page: "tatum".</meta>

->E P I S T O L A<-

Though opinions may vary, with the ancient serpent <note>A traditional biblical reference to the Devil or Satan.</note> fanning the flames, the resulting calamity is not nearly so deplorable as that which follows from the persuasion—once imbibed through his instinct—concerning that kind of evil which certain demented old women, whom they call <margin>Witches. Sorceresses.</margin> **Lamiae** <note>original: "Lamias"; a term from classical mythology for child-devouring demons, used here for witches.</note> or **Sagas** <note>original: "sagas"; wise-women or female fortune-tellers, often used pejoratively.</note>, are believed to inflict upon men and beasts without the drinking or application of any actual poison. For while from the former disputes various disagreements arise here and there according to men's affections, or as each person seems to abound in his own judgment, or according to the weight and quality of the talent granted by God; nevertheless, these often will not have such great importance as to touch the salvation of the soul in any way, or even to entirely disturb or break off friendships. 

How truly execrable, however, is the alienation from God and the most intimate bond with the demon—how great the hatreds among neighbors, how quarrelsome the factions in vicinities, what rivalries among peasants, what dissensions in cities, and how frequent the slaughters of the innocent—which that most fertile calamity gives birth to, with the <margin><unclear>Dissension.</unclear></margin> devil acting as the father of the tragedy.

<summary>The author argues that while intellectual or theological disputes are manageable, the superstitious belief in the supernatural powers of "witches" leads to social ruin, the murder of innocents, and a literal pact with the devil.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, Lamiae, Sagas, social discord, superstition, devil's influence, legal injustice</keywords>

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE
<sig>a 3</sig>

Daily experience teaches us that the mother of all [superstition], namely the opinion conceived regarding the prodigious power of the <term>Witches'</term> <note>original: "Lamiarum"</note> <term>evil-doing</term> <note>original: "maleficij" — specifically harmful magic performed through a pact, as opposed to simple poisoning</note> (I do not say <term>poisoning</term> <note>original: "ueneficij"</note>), is widespread. And since there are few diseases whose causes the common people—perversely instructed in the Christian religion—do not attribute to the work of Witches, there are hardly any others found to whom this entire business of impiety is more thoroughly known, or upon whom a more just occasion for taking action falls, than the physicians. Their minds are so disturbed and their ears so grated by this kind of incredulity that nothing resounds as loudly among the sick as that biting and false accusation of innocent poor women for the infliction of such an evil. 

<margin>5.</margin>
<margin>§. 6.</margin>

For some time, I hoped that this <term>Camarina</term> <note>A proverbial reference to a dangerous marsh in Sicily; "to move Camarina" meant to stir up an underlying evil or a nuisance that should be left alone.</note>, which exhales such a virulent stench, would gradually perish entirely through sound instruction from the Word of God. Instead, I experience more and more every day that it has been violently stirred up again, so that it exhales the virus of contagion far and wide to the ruin of many, while the spirit of storms blows horribly. Such vigilance as—

<summary>The author argues that physicians are uniquely positioned to witness the harmful social effects of witchcraft superstitions, specifically the false accusations leveled against innocent women by the sick. He laments that despite religious instruction, these beliefs are spreading like a contagious plague.</summary>

<keywords>witchcraft, medicine, false accusations, superstition, social contagion, maleficium, physicians</keywords>

Whenever that old knave <note>The devil</note> observes an opportunity, he acts while those whose duty it was to shatter his ramparts and utterly overthrow them—day and night, with the engines of Gospel doctrine—instead sleepily permit his crafts to succeed. For this reason, I have seen fit to perform a worthwhile service, while almost all theologians wink in silence at this grave impiety; while physicians tolerate false opinions regarding the causes of diseases and their impious cures; and while legal experts <term>Jurisconsults; those learned in the law</term> pronounce judgments here based on mere persuasion, which, through a long series of years and established custom, have not been so much examined as they have been confirmed as if by a prejudice beyond contradiction. Nor is any man heard to set his hand to healing this fatal wound or to explaining this labyrinth, to the ruin of many. Therefore, even if I am like "a jackdaw among the Muses" <note>original: "κολοιὸς ἐν ταῖς μούσαις" (koloiós en taîs moúsais); a Greek proverb for an unlearned person intruding upon the arts</note>, I may at least shake others from their lethargy with my chattering. I shall provide some handle for more deeply scrutinizing and discussing this difficult matter—which is a supreme insult to our Christian religion—through a more detailed deduction and such demonstration as I can offer.

A base opinion is a stain that cannot be cleansed.

Although I am not unaware that the stubbornness of a base opinion held without reason is a stain that cannot be cleansed <note>original: "inexpiabilem... tincturam"</note> and one that cannot be washed away, it is skillfully judged by our Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> in these words: "There is no dye so hard to wash out as the passion of those who cling, without reasoning, to wretched doctrines; for it is not possible to change the minds of those brought up in them." <note>original: "ἐστὶ δὲ οὐδεμία βαφὴ δυσσποιὸς οὕτως, ὡς τὸ τῶν ἄνευ λογισμοῦ πρὸς τὰ μοχθηρὰ δόγματα πάθος· οὐ γάρ ἐστι μεταπεῖσαι τοὺς αὐτοῖς ἐντραφέντας."</note> For he believes that those so educated cannot be led back to a sound mind or to the fruit of truth. I do not deny that it is just as difficult to adapt a new idea to the common mind and the general agreement of men.

<margin>
>>
/
</margin>
Nor, however, shall anyone disparage this undertaking of mine as if I—being too much a Suffenus <note>A character from Roman poetry used to represent someone who is conceited and overestimates their own meager talent</note> and insufficiently aware of my own insignificance—were rashly presuming to understand or be capable of anything more than others. How "scant is my household furniture" <note>original: "curta supellex"; a Roman idiom meaning a lack of mental resources or knowledge</note>, I know well, and no one knows it more surely than I; and this I know: that I know nothing. No one is being prejudged here. Added to this are my daily medical duties and constant travels, which certainly cut short the leisure that ought to be devoted to such nighttime studies <term>Lucubrations; scholarly works produced by candlelight or during the quiet hours of the night</term>. For this reason, during the previous hunting expeditions established at Hambach... <note>The text cuts off here as the author begins to describe the circumstances under which he wrote this work</note>

# ->E P I S T L E<-

...ties, while I was serving Your Highness and your illustrious and noble offspring by virtue of my office, I devoted myself primarily to this study.

I freely admit, therefore, that countless others could have surpassed this "infancy" <note>original: "infantiam"; here referring to his humble or unpolished work</note> of mine by infinite measures—through a deeper investigation of the truth, a clearer and more learned style of speech, and a more evident and forceful <note>original: "neruosa"; literally "sinewy" or vigorous</note> demonstration—owing to their keenness of intellect, excellence of learning, and greater abundance of leisure. But I hope that those gifted minds will be provoked by my meager writing, so that by speaking out they may instruct me more correctly (which is usually the fruit of such scholarly comparisons); or, by remaining silent, this opinion of mine, though it leaps a double octave <note>original: "δὶς διὰ πασῶν" (dis dia pason); an ancient Greek musical term for the widest interval, used here as a metaphor for a radical departure from conventional thought</note> away from the opinions ingrained in that superstitious <note>original: "religioso"; in this context, it likely refers to an age bound by overly scrupulous or uncritical traditional beliefs</note> age, may seem to be approved. By this reasoning, I trust I shall have gained a sufficiently rich interest from my labors; nor will I regret the effort spent, whether I am recalled to the knowledge of truth by sounder teaching, or confirmed in this rare opinion heard by few.

<margin>Truth is hidden in the depths.</margin>
Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) famous for the atomic theory and for the observation that truth is hidden at the bottom of a well</note> taught most correctly that Nature has hidden truth deep in the abyss; to seek this out more vigilantly, [to investigate...] <meta>catchword: inuesti- (to investigate)</meta>

# ->D E D I C A T O R Y<-

it is proper to investigate and search out. For this is indeed joined with greater fairness than to stubbornly defend an opinion that one has rashly embraced.

<margin>The theological argument of the work.</margin>
The subject matter is partly theological, since the devil’s efforts are exposed by the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, and the safest way to counter them is taught. <margin>Philosophical.</margin> It is also partly philosophical, in that the vanity of Satan's deceptions and the corrupted imagination of witches are refuted by natural reasoning. <margin>Medical.</margin> Likewise, it is partly medical, where it is demonstrated that diseases, their causes, and symptoms—wrongly attributed to witches <note>original: "Lamijs"; referring here to the *Lamiae*, a term often used in this period to denote witches or night-demons</note>—arise according to the laws of nature. <margin>Legal.</margin> It also partly concerns the principles of jurisprudence <term>jurisprudence: the theory or philosophy of law</term>, since it treats the punishment of infamous magicians, witches, and poisoners <note>original: "ueneficorum"; refers to both sorcerers and those who use toxic potions</note> according to the quality and magnitude of the crime, in a manner different from what has been practiced until now.

However, lest I be thought to have rashly and stubbornly overstepped the bounds of my own talent and the limits of my profession by trusting too much in my own brain, I presented these paradoxes <note>original: "παράδοξα" (paradoxa); statements or opinions that run contrary to common belief or expectation</note> of mine to many most learned men, even from

<summary>The author outlines the multidisciplinary nature of his work, explaining how it combines theology, philosophy, medicine, and law to challenge prevailing superstitions about witchcraft. He argues that what are commonly thought to be demonic illnesses are actually natural medical conditions.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, theology, natural philosophy, medical diagnosis, legal reform, jurisprudence, Satan's deceptions, paradoxes</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's dedication to his patron. On the previous page, the author explained that he seeks the truth regarding witchcraft through theology, philosophy, medicine, and law, rather than blindly following tradition. He concluded by mentioning that he had submitted his "paradoxes" (unconventional views) to the learned men of the patron's court for review.</meta>

# ->E P I S T L E<-

to the men of your Highness's household—theologians, legal experts, and most excellent colleagues—with the intention that they be read and examined. My goal was that through their judgment, these ideas might be corrected, changed, or allowed to stand—or otherwise fall and be rejected.

<margin>The Hammer of Witches, p.</margin>
If anyone should object that the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum"; the most famous and influential treatise on the prosecution of witches, published in 1486</note> has already completed this labor, I beg him to read the absurdities, ineptitudes, and often even impieties collected in that book by the theologians Heinrich Institoris <note>also known as Heinrich Kramer</note> and Jakob Sprenger. Let him compare their work with this writing of ours, setting aside all prejudice, and judge; he will understand that I maintain and defend an entirely different, indeed contrary, position. For I have no desire to "unweave Penelope’s web" <note>a classical proverb referring to Penelope from the *Odyssey*, who delayed suitors by unravelling her shroud every night; here it means to redo work already done or engage in futile labor</note> or to do what has already been finished.

To be sure, Ulrich Molitor, a counselor to King Sigismund of Bohemia, said a few things on this subject in his *Dialogues on Witches and Soothsayers* <term>soothsayers: those who predict the future, here translating "Pythonicis", a reference to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</term>. Giovanni Francesco Pico also wrote something concerning witches <note>original: "Strigibus"; a term for night-witches or malevolent spirits often associated with owls</note>. Likewise, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, proposed five questions to Emperor Maximilian. However, the nature of their judgment will become evident through a comparison with our own work.

<meta>catchword: Furthermore</meta>

<summary>The author explains that he submitted his work to experts for peer review and explicitly distances himself from the Malleus Maleficarum, which he critiques as absurd and impious. He acknowledges previous authors on the subject but asserts that his own judgment and conclusions are distinct and superior.</summary>

### ->DEDICATORY<-

# ->E P I S T L E<-

Furthermore, beyond the many reasons that urged me to dedicate this modest offspring of mine to your Highness <note>original: "tuæ Celsitudini" (your Highness)</note>, this one especially encouraged me: that since I have now been your Highness’s physician for thirteen years, I have frequently heard various opinions in your court regarding the power and incantations of the "witches" <term>witches: translating "Lamiae," a term for female monsters or sorceresses believed to harm children and cast spells</term> who have recently reappeared in your vast territories. Yet, it has hardly been possible to learn a more certain view from anyone—one more in harmony with my own and more deeply drawn from the fountains of truth—than that which I have several times heard from your Highness’s own lips with these ears (I am compelled to admit it, whether I wish to or not). 

This view is, of course: that witches can harm no one through any malicious will, dire imprecation, or evil gaze. Rather, their imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> is corrupted by the hidden effort of a demon, and because they are agitated as if by melancholy <term>melancholy: in early medicine, an excess of "black bile" thought to cause depression, delusions, and mental instability</term>, they convince themselves that whatever evils have been brought about by Satan himself—or by natural occurrence according to the hidden plan of God—were committed by them. For when the manner of their actions is weighed in the balance, and their instruments are examined with careful <margin>scrutiny</margin>...

<meta>catchword: scrutiny (spectio)</meta>

<summary>The author, Johann Weyer, praises his patron’s enlightened view that "witches" do not actually possess supernatural powers but are instead suffering from demonic delusions and melancholy. Weyer argues that the harms attributed to these women are actually caused by Satan or natural providence, not by the women's spells.</summary>

<keywords>witches, Lamiae, melancholy, imagination, demon, Satan, medical diagnosis, Duke William of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, legal responsibility, delusions</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Duke William of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. On the previous page, the author began explaining the Duke's skeptical stance on witchcraft: that "witches" are actually suffering from mental delusions (melancholy) orchestrated by demons, rather than possessing real supernatural power. This page elaborates on the legal and moral consequences of that view.</meta>

# ->E P I S T L E<-

<meta>continuity: ...scrutiny</meta>

scrutiny, the impossibility <note>original: "ἀδυνατία" (adynatia)</note> and falsehood of the whole matter soon becomes clearer than the light of day to all eyes. Your Highness learnedly, prudently, and piously concedes that poisoning <term>poisoning: translating "veneficium," a term that historically blurred the line between magical "hexing" and physical poisoning; Weyer argues here for the strictly physical definition</term> is committed only by female poisoners <note>original: "φαρμακευτρίαις" (pharmakeutriais)</note> or male poisoners, through poison that is either drunk or smeared on, resulting in the harmful destruction of humans and animals. If the crime is then established beyond a doubt, your Highness wills that the requirements of the laws <margin>Romans 13</margin> be satisfied.

# JOHANN BRACHELIUS, LICENTIATE OF LAWS
## To the Reader.

When God established the spacious scrolls of the immense heaven,
And suspended the lands in the midst of the air,
Adorning the pole with stars, and the atmosphere with clouds:
He likewise created for himself servants, divine
Beings, to carry his commands through the gentle breezes,
And who would spend their ages far from earthly cares.
From their number, the most just Father thrust one—
Who so deserved it—from heaven down to the Stygian waters: <note>original: "Stygias... ad undas"; a reference to the River Styx, here signifying Hell.</note>
There, bound by manacles and hard fetters,
He sits for the punishment of his crimes, and will sit eternally,
Paying the sad penalties for the guilt he committed.
<margin>
Observe the history, how great, page... <note>original: "obs Historia qñta, p." These are likely abbreviated notes for the reader to cross-reference the history of the fallen angels in the main text.</note>
</margin>
Yet what frauds, and what wicked arts, meanwhile,
Does he prepare for the wretched day and night? What nets does he spread?
Or what is he capable of? If by chance you care to know,
Read this work, Reader, the monuments of the learned Weyer: <note>original: "Vuieri," the Latinized form of Weyer.</note>
From here you will carry away what is desired; from here you will teach yourself your own wishes.
Moreover, it tells what trust should be attributed
To magical things, provided that cruel poisons are absent;
Or by what art you may heal one oppressed by sorceries, <term>veneficijs: acts of poisoning or harmful magic.</term>
Or what sufficiently worthy punishment the furious race
Of witches <term>Sagarum: plural of "saga," a wise-woman or witch.</term> pays under the judge—all this he relates in a wondrous order.
But why you, memorable Weyer, have taken up
Such great labors, I cannot yet truly discern well enough.
"The public good," you say, "moved me." But who
Cares for the public good now? Who commonly respects
Noble hearts, and pays deserved honors to their achievements?
You, however, shall console your too-weary mind with this:
That your fame shall not die at any time.

It concludes by acknowledging that Weyer’s selfless dedication to the public good will earn him eternal fame despite a thankless public.</summary>

I confess indeed that I have undertaken a truly arduous task, and one far exceeding the strength of my small ability, wherein I dare to step forth onto the stage and struggle with fraudulent spirits—the powerful lords of this world—since they possess so many incomprehensible ways of deceiving, and so many tunnels and hidden retreats for escaping. On account of the subtlety of their essence, the swiftness of their motion, the experience of their very long lives, and the perversity of their will, they elude our earthly thickness far and wide, so that by whatever arguments you attack them, you clearly see that you have been cheated. ### TO THE READER.

b,, 4,,

...whether they strike, or by their arrangement, they harm humans or beasts. Thus it will be understood that there is a vast difference between profane magicians, witches <term>Lamiae: here meaning elderly women who are victims of demonic delusion rather than practitioners of real magic</term>, and poisoners <term>veneficos: those who use physical toxins to harm, often confused with supernatural sorcerers</term>: about whom, however, as if they were the same, there has been much confusion in how they are treated, debated, and sentenced until now. 

In order that these things might become more clearly known, in the **Third Book** <margin>BOOK III</margin>, I put forward those who are thought to be afflicted by the witchcraft <note>original: "maleficio"</note> of witches, demonstrating that they are all troubled by demons or are possessed through the hidden permission of God, without any cooperation from any witch or any other human being.

From here, in proper order, in the **Fourth Book** <margin>BOOK IV</margin>, I turn to the cure <margin><insert>Cure for witchcraft</insert></margin> of those believed to be crushed by this kind of witchcraft—a treatment infinitely different from what has been observed up to this point. Here, whatever illicit cures have been devised by demons to strengthen their own kingdom—through forbidden conjurations, characters <note>original: "characteres"; magical sigils or signs</note>, bindings <note>original: "ligaturas"; the practice of tying knots to cast spells, often for impotence</note>, amulets or charms worn on the body, rings, seals, images, and similar shadowy madnesses—are refuted and cast out by the authority of Holy Scripture and the weight of reason.

...business might be handled more incorruptibly and with a more sincere conscience. This was the chief goal of the labor I have undertaken in this work.

<margin>Summary!</margin> However, I have been occupied for a long time in this grave meditation—more than can be expressed—and I have been tortured by immense pains (as He knows, from whom nothing is hidden) because I saw those demented old women, deluded by the demon, commonly called witches <term>Lamias: here, the author refers to women who believe they have supernatural powers due to demonic delusion, rather than actual criminal intent</term>. Even though they had committed no extraordinary crime (for I am not speaking here of poisoners <term>veneficis: those who use physical toxins or drugs to cause harm</term>), I saw them in many places being thrown so atrociously and without any pity into dark and squalid prisons—dreadful lodgings of shadows and dwellings of demons. From there, I saw them being brutally dragged to the place of execution <term>carnificinam: literally the "butcher's bench" or place of torture and death</term>, and finally rashly thrown to be devoured by flames. I saw that the confessions of these insane little old women were being relied upon as truth, and that not enough distinction was being made between these deluded witches and actual poisoners. Meanwhile, I saw sacrilegious magicians <term>Magos: practitioners of high ritual or ceremonial magic</term>, who were severely punished under the Old Law <note>A reference to Mosaic Law, such as Exodus 22:18 or Leviticus 20:27</note>, now living with more impunity—indeed, even with praise among many. Therefore, I could not—driven by the logic of the argument and the impulse of my conscience—do anything other than add my opinion on this matter, such as it is, to these four books. In a **Fifth Book** <margin>FIFTH</margin>, serving as a sort of appendix, I shall declare what I feel, and the reasons upon which I lean, concerning the punishment of infamous magicians <term>Magorum infamium</term>, according to the truth of **CHRIST**...

# ON THE DEVIL,
## HIS ORIGIN,
### ENDEAVOR AND POWER, Book I.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring ornate floral patterns and scrolling vines, with a small human figure or cherub nestled within the design.</image-desc>

Intending to explain the deceptions and incantations of demons, I shall begin with their primary author, the devil, and his arts, efforts, and power. My purpose is that once he is known, and his authority and reputation are thoroughly understood, a more evident judgment may be formed regarding all his works. Thus, every person may be able to look into all his actions with a clear eye of the mind, and henceforth perceive them more deeply and with less hindrance.

<margin>Aristotle thought that demons do not exist.</margin>
<margin>The Platonists invented many things concerning demons.</margin>
Embracing the sacred doctrine of the Christian religion and the confession of an undoubting faith, I utterly reject the decrees of **Aristotle** and the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>, who contend that demons do not exist in the natural world. Likewise, I am unable to entirely approve of the fictitious distinctions of **Plato**, nor can I subscribe to the opinions of **Porphyry**, **Psellus**, **Proclus**, **Plotinus**, or **Iamblichus** <note>Neoplatonist philosophers and writers who developed complex hierarchies of spirits</note>. While they wrote copiously about demons, they wrote as if they were recording a historical account of a real event, describing many things they never actually saw.

<margin>Genesis 1. Hebrews 1. When the angels were created.</margin>
Therefore, I believe that the omnipotent architect of the universe, God, before the construction of this visible world, beautifully adorned and established that incorporeal realm into admirable orders of spirits for His service. This we know from **Moses**, the envoy of the divine Majesty...

# On the Illusions of Demons

...[sacred] images <note>This completes the word "sacris" from the previous page. Tertullian is arguing that demons claim the credit for divinity by lurking around idols and temple sacrifices.</note> offered to them, and which is for him a more refined pasture, by which he may turn man away from the thought of true divinity with false illusions; I shall explain how he carries these out. *Every spirit is winged.* <note>original: "Omnis spiritus ales est." <margin>Psellus on demons. <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078) was a Byzantine monk and scholar whose work "De Operatione Daemonum" (On the Operation of Demons) was a primary source for Renaissance demonologists.</note></margin>
However, a certain Marcus—a distinguished devotee of the demonic world who lived a solitary life in the Chersonese <note>The Gallipoli Peninsula in modern-day Turkey</note> bordering Greece—explained a more extensive method and manner of doing those things we have mentioned, and other similar things, to Michael Psellus. 

Demons (he says), although they lack biological sex and a language of their own, nevertheless change that airy body <note>The "aereal body" was a common Neoplatonic concept; it was believed demons were composed of a refined substance that, while material, was as thin and invisible as air.</note> granted to them into various forms at their will—just like clouds when the wind blows—and they contract and extend it, in the same way that seems to happen to earthworms on account of their finer substance and ease of movement. And not only does a diversity in size occur in them, but they also vary their figures and colors into many forms. For the body of a demon is prepared by nature for both. Insofar as its nature is easily yielding, it is thus transformed into various species of shapes; but insofar as it is airy, it takes on different colors like the air itself. 

But while air is colored from the outside, the body of the demon changes the appearance of its colors according to the emotions of its mind, just as a human's does—but far better, as it is more obedient to the soul <note>Meaning the demon's physical form reacts instantly to its internal thoughts or desires, much like a human face flushes with anger, but with total control over the entire body's shape.</note>. However, everything dissolves quickly because of the body’s mobility and thinness. Thus, it appears as a man, and soon after it turns up as a woman; it roars like a lion, leaps like a leopard, barks like a dog, and sometimes transforms itself into the shape of a skin-bag or a vessel.

*It is pleasing to appropriately insert a rather elegant story at this point. Helinand the monk relates that he heard from his paternal uncle Ebaudus—who was a chamberlain to Henry, the Archbishop of Reims and brother of King Louis of France—that while Archbishop Henry was taking a midday nap <note>original: "somnum meridianum." The practice of the siesta was common, but in this literature, the "noonday devil" or supernatural events often occur during this time.</note> on a journey one summer, a certain soldier among the rest of the company fell asleep after lunch with his mouth wide open. From his mouth, those who were awake saw a certain small, white beast, similar to a weasel, emerge and run forward to a nearby stream. When it had run anxiously up and down the bank of the stream and found no way to cross, one of the bystanders approached and placed his unsheathed sword over the narrow stream, making a sort of bridge of it. The little beast immediately crossed the stream over the sword, ran further off, and hid itself from view. A little later it was seen returning; when it looked for the familiar bridge again and found it had been removed, it ran about, unable to cross. The same man as before again joined the banks of the stream by laying down his sword, and then moved away. Then the little beast crossed, and returning to the still-gaping mouth of the sleeper, it entered while everyone watched. Immediately, the man who had been sleeping woke up. When asked whether he had experienced anything in his sleep, he replied that he was tired and weary, as if from a difficult and long journey, in which he had twice crossed a river over an iron bridge. From this, his companions concluded that he had truly dreamed of the very things they had seen. ...an apparition <note>original: "idolon." <margin>The mind of the philosopher Athenodorus, strengthened against the terrors of the demon.</margin>

The philosopher Athenodorus <note>Athenodorus Cananites (c. 74 BC–7 AD), a Stoic philosopher and teacher of the Emperor Augustus.</note> came to Athens and read the notice. Having heard the price, and because the extreme cheapness was suspicious, he made inquiries and was told the whole story. Nevertheless—or rather, all the more because of it—he rented the house. When evening began to fall, he ordered a bed to be prepared for him in the front part of the house; he called for his writing tablets, his stylus, and a light, and sent all his servants into the inner rooms. He focused his mind, his eyes, and his hand on writing, so that a vacant mind might not imagine the phantoms he had heard of or invent empty fears for itself.

At first, there was the silence of night, just as it is everywhere. Then, the clatter of iron was heard, and the rattling of chains. He did not lift his eyes or set down his stylus; instead, he steeled his mind and used it to shield his ears. Then the noise grew louder and approached; it was heard now as if at the threshold, and now as if within the room. He looked back, saw it, and recognized the figure that had been described to him. It was standing there, beckoning with its finger, like someone calling to him. He, in response, signaled with his hand for it to wait a little while, and once again bent over his wax tablets and stylus. The ghost rattled its chains over the head of the man as he wrote; he looked back again and saw it beckoning as before...

Three deceptions

...they are not at all less frequent than they once were, through the manifest deceptions of demons. There are two kinds of these spirits. For some are mild, and might rightly be called household spirits <note>original: *Lares familiares*. In ancient Roman tradition, the Lares were protective spirits of the home and family.</note>; they are active in houses especially in the dead of night, and they seem to be heard performing the duties of servants—specifically descending the stairs, opening doors, tending the fire, drawing water, preparing food, and whatever else is customary in a particular house—though in fact they do absolutely nothing at all. Many of these also have foreknowledge of future events through hidden signs, and are heard performing tasks beforehand that we find completed shortly afterward; for instance, they announce by signs that merchants will soon arrive to bring goods for sale. I observed this myself several times as a child in my father’s house, quite terrified; a huge store of hops <note>original: *lupuli*. Hops were a vital agricultural commodity for brewing beer, often stored in large quantities in attics.</note> was kept in the attic, and whenever buyers were about to arrive, the sacks would be heard being thrown down the stairs on the preceding night, in the exact same manner that the following day proved to be the reality. This was always greeted with applause as a lucky omen. For when merchants decide on their affairs, intending to travel somewhere for business, they speak of it beforehand and announce they are starting a journey for that purpose. The devil, understanding this, displays his mockeries to those the merchants are traveling toward before they actually arrive. The distance between locations provides the necessary time. In this way, the demon seems both to have known beforehand and to foretell what has already begun to occur. Others are grim,

<margin>Little Mountain Men <note>original German: "Bergmännlein"</note></margin>
...dwarves, three-quarters [of a cubit] <note>A "dodrans" is a Roman unit of measure representing three-quarters of a foot. They appear to be little old men and are dressed in the style of miners—that is, wearing a belted tunic and a leather apron hanging around their loins. These spirits do not usually cause harm to the miners, but wander about in the shafts and tunnels; and though they actually do nothing, they seem to occupy themselves with every kind of labor, as if now they were digging at the veins, now pouring the excavated ore into vessels, or now turning the hoisting machine. Although they sometimes harass the workers with pebbles, they very rarely hurt them. Nor do they ever strike unless they have first been provoked by laughter or curses.

Therefore, they are not much different from those demons who rarely appear to men, even though they daily perform a portion of the household chores and tend to the livestock. <margin>The difference of demons according to the philosophers. 1 2 3</margin>
The philosophers who believed that demons exist divided them in three ways. Some think they are all immortal, evil, and weak: such as Psellus, who being a Christian, subscribed to the opinion of Christians. Others think some are mortal, some good, and some evil; they are powerful, yet they look out for themselves through a fear of death. The third is the distinction of the Platonists, who affirm that they are immortal and powerful, and familiar to us, being partly good and partly evil. To all this there is a consensus among the philosophers that demons are natural beings, whom Plato places in charge of poisonings, incantations, magic, <term>goeteia <note>original: γοητεία; a Greek term for "low" magic or sorcery, often involving the manipulation of spirits, as opposed to high religious ritual.</note></term>, the arts of priests, and oracles.

<margin>The distinction between good and evil demons.</margin>
Furthermore, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians."</note> distinguishes good demons from evil ones more clearly and openly than Proclus. He says: "Gods, angels, and good demons do not appear in a ghostly manner <note>original: *phantastico modo*</note>, but in a way that is entirely their own and true. But evil spirits appear in a ghostly and deceptive way; they mimic the presence of gods and good demons. For this reason, they command their worshiper to be just, so that they themselves might seem good, just like the gods. However, because they are evil by nature, when they are asked to bring about evil, they do so willingly, and they lead us toward unjust things. These are the ones who lie and deceive even in oracles, and who advise and carry out shameful deeds."

<margin>Plato</margin>

For tell me, I ask you, what use is there in showing walking statues? Therefore, the evil one is unable to perform those signs which benefit the salvation of men and confer something good upon humanity.

<margin>*Limits of action are established for the devil.*</margin>
And although God, by His own counsel and according to what we deserve, sometimes permits the demon to exercise his mockeries and tyranny against men of every rank, He does not however indulge him or turn a blind eye to everything. Nor does He grant him an infinite license restricted by no boundaries; otherwise, we would all perish, killed by the devil in a single moment.

...which are still in the blade <note>original: "in herba," referring to young crops that have not yet matured.</note>, or to transplant sown harvests elsewhere; he cannot love honest and good men, nor hate the wicked; he cannot look into or fully understand the senses and thoughts of men—contrary to what Plato suggests in his *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato or his circle concerning the study of wisdom and the nature of the cosmos.</note>; he cannot insert hard, rough, or sharp materials through solid parts of the body without injury, or through narrower passages that do not correspond to the size of the materials in certain proportion or dimension according to the laws of nature; he cannot be compelled toward any evil (to which he himself, being entirely evil day and night, is already naturally inclined by a malicious will that surpasses even the worst of mortals) by any man's command, art, or by any pact; he cannot sneak into human bodies by his own will, or at the whim or curse of some malicious and idle old woman <note>original: "maleferiatæ anus." ...always a belly-speaker: <note>original Greek: ἐγγαστρίμυθος (*engastrimythos*), a term for one who speaks from the stomach.</note> except that in the fourth book of Kings, chapters 21 and 23, it is interpreted as a "wanter" or "one who wills," <note>original Greek: θελητής (*theletes*). In truth, the word **אוב** *Ob* signifies among the Hebrews a leather skin-bottle or a flask. From this, that nation called those demons *Ob* (or in the plural, *Oboth*) who gave responses in muffled voices from the more remote parts of the human body—such as from the armpits or the female private parts—as if the sound were coming out of a skin-bottle or a small jar.

The Greeks, however, using a more fitting term, called them *engastrimythoi* or *engastritai* because they are brought forth from the bellies of men. Certain Latin writers, imitating this Greek term, have not ineptly called them **ventriloquists**. <note>original Latin: *ventriloquos*. Literally "belly-talkers."</note> These names are properly applied to the evil spirits themselves, yet they are also sometimes used for the people who suffer them.

A demon of this kind once made a certain magician named Eurycles famous among the Athenians, as Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes (c. 446–386 BCE) was the greatest comic playwright of ancient Athens.</note> testifies in *The Wasps*. There, he says that he brought much benefit to the Republic of the Athenians through his substituted comedies, which—imitating the oracle and manner of Eurycles—he took care to have recited secretly by entering into the bellies of other poets. From that Eurycles (as the most learned Greek commentaries show), prophets of that kind were afterwards called *Eurycleitai*, as well as *engastrimythoi* or *engastritai*.

I also remember reading that the famous Delphic oracle <note>The most important oracle in the ancient Greek world, where the priestess (the Pythia) delivered prophecies believed to come from Apollo.</note> used to be delivered from the private parts of a woman. Furthermore, Saint Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE), an influential Christian theologian.</note>—in the book he composed *On Christian Doctrine*—is the authority who states that the girl mentioned in the sixteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles <note>Acts 16:16 mentions a slave girl with a "spirit of Python" who earned money by fortune-telling.</note> was a ventriloquist. It must be completely exterminated from the ranks of divine Medicine, since it has defiled both with its feigned exorcisms, its prayers of barbaric words <note>original: "barbaricarum uocum," referring to "voces magicae," or nonsense words used in spells</note>, the recitation of obscure names, the abuse of sacred scripture, ligatures <note>magical knots or bindings used in charms</note>, amulets, and incantations intended for the destruction of human health and life. We read that the more secret interpretation of the divine law among the Jews, called **Kabbalah**, has been repeatedly defiled and corrupted by this magic in the same way; indeed, the treacherous Jews do not shrink from asserting that **Christ** performed his incomparable miracles by means of such "Cabalistic Magic."

## On the Deceptions of Demons

...shadows <note>Completing the word *tenebras* from the previous page</note> to be summoned forth, and (as Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), author of *The Golden Ass*, who was famously tried for using magic to win a wealthy wife</note> says) agile souls to return, the sluggish sea to be bound, and new bodies to be created. By the singular goodness of God, these have now been shaken from human memory for the benefit of mankind and utterly abolished; God will eventually wish them to be completely removed. Indeed, the number of these deceptive actions and things is immense, and it is better that they remain hidden. At the very least, it is useful to forewarn the cautious and overly credulous, lest they be deceived and seduced by divine names impiously dragged into the matter, or by the words of Holy Scripture wickedly twisted. 

We have noticed this happening until now: men use these things as a pretext to purge and excuse themselves of the gravest offenses, claiming they are merely invoking sacrosanct names and mingling the Word of God in this diabolical workshop. In such a place, the most holy name of God is profaned by a horrible crime, and divine Scripture is defiled by abominable abuse.

# On the Illusions of Demons
<meta>catchword: Stenogra-</meta>

*...graphy <note>Johannes Trithemius’s *Steganographia* (written c. 1499), a work that disguised systems of cryptography as methods of summoning spirits to transmit messages</note> cursorily, reading the beginnings of several chapters. I barely held the book in my hands for two hours before I threw it away immediately, because I began to be terrified by such great conjurations <note>original: *adiurationes*</note> and such barbarous and unusual names of spirits (I should perhaps say demons). All such names—as far as I could see—are in unknown languages. For they are either Arabic, Hebrew, Chaldean, or Greek; there was little or no Latin. Furthermore, there are countless symbols <note>original: *characteres*, referring to occult sigils or magical scripts</note> by which individual conjurations are marked.*

*Regarding what Trithemius writes in his letter to Arnold Bostius <note>A Carmelite monk and friend of Trithemius to whom the author revealed his secret work</note>—that the words are plain and clear, without any transposition of letters or words, so that all may read and understand them, yet his secret (whatever it may be) remains unknown—in this, he may have spoken the truth. For throughout this Steganography, he inserts the most holy and pious prayers everywhere, to be sent to a friend in place of letters; but in truth, these are crocodile tears <note>A common metaphor for deceptive or false displays of piety intended to mask a darker purpose</note>. For he seems to me to do what Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher; the author refers to his 7th Epistle</note> thought of Apollophanes in his letter to Sosipater: "He wickedly uses divine things against God, and through worldly and empty wisdom, he strives to nullify divine wisdom." <note>original: *Diuinis aduersus Deum nephariè utitur, ac per mundanam inanemq; sapientiam, diuinam sapientiam euacuare molitur*</note>*

*As for his promise that he will perform all things without the aid of spirits, he truly (as Daniel says) "fashions lies against his own head."* <margin>Daniel 13 <note>A reference to the Story of Susanna in the biblical Apocrypha, where Daniel exposes lying elders who are then "cut in two" as punishment</note></margin> *I believe a good angel of God remains to cut him in two and dissolve the wicked covenant <note>original: *foedus iniquum*</note> which he has entered into and ratified with harmful angels, as is clearly declared by the work itself.* <margin>The order of the Steganography</margin> *Furthermore, if I remember correctly, this same man...*

### Book Two.

<margin>Note Well</margin>
<margin>Twelve Imperial Spirits</margin>
That Steganography <note>original: *Stenographia*. In this context, it refers to Johannes Trithemius's system of "hidden writing" which used the names of spirits as a cryptographic key</note> maintains a specific order: first, it arranges the names of the spirits themselves; next, it sets out their **conjurations** <note>original: *adiurationes*; formal commands or rituals used to summon or bind spirits</note>; and it records the **symbols** <note>original: *characteres*; specifically, the occult sigils or marks associated with individual entities</note> of each one. Finally, it distinguishes certain figures from which one may draw and elicit the appropriate names of spirits for individual conjurations, whenever the need arises. Furthermore, it divides the spirits in these figures into four ranks: ***Emperors, Dukes, Counts, and Servants***. He claims there are only twelve Emperors of the entire world, just as the philosophers teach there are twelve winds. From these, he designates four as the primary ones—of the ***East, South, West, and North***—whom he calls the "Great Emperors."

<margin>360 <unclear>or</unclear> 480 Dukes</margin>
<margin>Counts</margin>
<margin>Servants</margin>
Under each Emperor, he establishes Dukes—I believe thirty or forty of them. Under each individual Duke, there are again Counts in greater number; and under the Counts, there are countless servants.

<margin>Note</margin>
In this manner, therefore, he applies his theory to the actual practice of his art. When he wishes to reveal his plans to a distant friend (for he calls these his "secrets"), he writes, in place of a letter, a certain prayer of miraculous holiness and devotion, though it is tainted by pretense <note>original: *fuco affectatam*; literally "painted with a cosmetic," suggesting the religious language is a deceptive mask</note>. He marks this with the symbol of one of the twelve Emperors and sends it to the friend who (as he says) knows the art. Having received the document, the friend opens it: and at the bottom of the letter, he first observes which Emperor’s symbol is present. If it is the Prince of the East, he turns toward the east and holds the letter open toward that region of the sky. He immediately searches his books for the conjurations by which that prince is compelled to send one of his subjects...

<margin>The origin of the surname Aenobarbus.</margin>
...it is handed down that they <note>The "Divine Youths" or Dioscuri, who according to legend appeared to Lucius Domitius</note> commanded him to announce to the Senate and the people a victory, concerning which there was still uncertainty. And to prove the truth of their word, they so stroked his cheeks that they turned his hair from black to a reddish-gold, similar to bronze <note>original: "æriq; similem"; the name Aenobarbus literally means "Bronze-beard"</note>: from which comes the surname **Aenobarbus**. **Suetonius** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), a Roman historian famous for his biographies of the first twelve emperors</note>.

<margin>Magicians and the possessed are sometimes transported.</margin>
This kind of men also has their own methods, by which they command wine or butter, after money has been counted out, to be brought from distant places by the work of **Satan**. It is also no wonder that magicians themselves, with whom the demon plays, are sometimes either suddenly transported or appear in such a way; since we know that many who are subject to the vexations of demons are sometimes carried elsewhere. Thus history tells that **Pythagoras** <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) who was famously said to be capable of bilocation</note> was at one and the same moment both in **Thurii** and in **Metapontum**, and furthermore that **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century wonder-worker often compared to Christ or portrayed as a magician</note> was translated most swiftly from **Smyrna** to **Ephesus** as soon as the word was spoken. Yet we rightly believe that every association with demons procured by whatever art, and the whole system of these delusions, is a **pestiferous fraud** <note>original: "pestiferam fraudem"</note>, introduced for the ultimate destruction of men.

At the end of the performance, complaining that he had collected too little money from mortals, he said that he wished to ascend into heaven. Thereupon, a rope having been thrown high up, the little horse followed into the heights; the illusionist, as if he were going to pull it back by the tail, also ascended. Then his wife, grabbing hold of her husband, followed him, and likewise the maidservant, so that they appeared to seek the air together in a continuous ascent, as if they were linked in a chain. While the people watched this in amazement, a certain citizen happened to be passing by and asked what on earth was happening there. The reply was that a street-performer was ascending into the air with a little horse. This man immediately asserted that he had just seen the performer in the street, going into an inn. When the spectators realized they had been tricked, they departed.

However, so that this tale and the power—or rather, the mockeries—of magicians may be more clearly exposed to everyone's sight and more deeply understood, come, let us contemplate with eyes that are not deceived. Let us investigate with skillful research the efforts, works, and power of **Pharaoh’s magicians** <note>A reference to the Book of Exodus, where Pharaoh's sorcerers competed with Moses and Aaron by turning staffs into serpents</note> or sorcerers. Everyone knows that a corpse could not reflect the magnificence of the gods; yet the female diviner <note>original: "diuinatrix" — referring to the Witch of Endor.</note> claimed that she saw "gods ascending from the earth" <note>This refers to 1 Samuel 28:13, where the woman tells Saul, "I see a divine being coming up out of the ground."</note>.

I do not wish to deny that it was easy for that one <margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin> who **transforms himself into an angel of light** to display the ghost of this most holy man—especially to a godless king and a lost little servant of Satan. <margin>Lekanomanteia <note>original Greek: Λεκανομαντεία. From 'lekane' (basin) and 'manteia' (prophecy).</note></margin> Psellus <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar known for his treatise on demonology.</note> describes *Lekanomanteia* [divination by basin] and says it was in use among the Assyrians; but it was also familiar to the Chaldeans and Egyptians, and even today the Turks use it, though somewhat differently. Golden and silver plates, and precious stones marked with certain characters, were placed into a basin filled with water. After the customary words were spoken by which the demon was summoned, the question was proposed. Then, first indeed, a thin sound without a voice was heard, which was the sign of the demon entering. Afterward, as the water overflowed, faint voices emerged from it, by which the question was answered; yet these were made intentionally very faint, lest the demon be convicted of lying in those things which it did not know.

<margin>Gastromanteia <note>original Greek: Γαστρομαντεία. Literally "belly-divination," but here referring to a form of hydromancy using glass vessels.</note></margin> *Gastromanteia* differed from the former in that it delivered responses not by voice, but by pictures. Round glass vessels, filled with the clearest water, were set out, and lighted wax candles were placed around them. When the evocation of the demon with a secret murmur was finished and the question presented, an untainted boy or a pregnant woman was employed to gaze intently and accurately into the glasses and look around, and to ask, command, and demand answers. These, finally, [revealed] by images in the water... <note>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "impressed" suggesting the next page describes how these images appear.</note>

<margin>Mirror divination <note>original Greek: Κατοπτρομαντεία (Katoptromanteia).</note></margin>
**Mirror divination** predicts the future using bright and polished mirrors, in which the images of the things being asked about shine forth, having been formed or reflected by the devil. The Emperor **Didius Julianus** <note>Didius Julianus (r. 193 AD) was a Roman emperor who famously bought the throne at auction from the Praetorian Guard; his short reign ended in his execution.</note> made use of this; and it is written that by the devil’s prompting, he foresaw many of the things that eventually happened to him.

<margin>Crystal divination <note>original Greek: χρυσταλλομαντεία (Crystallomanteia).</note></margin>
**Crystal divination** is performed using crafted and polished crystals. The devil plays a part in these—for in many of them he lurks hidden in a minute form, or sometimes disguised as another material—and he reports back to his followers (almost as if prophesying) the signs and figures of events or the sought-after matters depicted there.

<margin>Ring divination <note>original Greek: δακτυλιομαντεία (Daktyliomanteia).</note></margin>
It is called **Ring divination** when sorcerers divine using rings crafted according to certain positions of the heavens or consecrated through a diabolical ritual. Yet, far too many people who use these forbidden modes of demonic divination live among those who bear the Christian name with total impunity.

<margin>Water divination <note>original Greek: ὑδρομαντεία (Hydromanteia).</note></margin>
**Water divination** was employed in various ways. A cup was filled with water, and a ring suspended by a thread was balanced from a finger over the water; then, with a set of spoken words, a declaration or confirmation of the matter being sought was requested. If the proposal was true, the ring would strike the cup a certain number of times by its own movement, without being pushed. They say that **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious and legal institutions.</note> practiced this and consulted the gods who were summoned into the water. There are other methods of this kind as well.

<page-num>164</page-num>
# On the Illusions of Demons

...those who flee to diviners or to the Pythian family <note>original: "Pythiam familiam" — a reference to the followers or methods of the Delphic Oracle (the Pythia), used here to mean any superstitious or demonic source of hidden knowledge</note>, it is to be feared that they will undergo a well-deserved punishment. It is not out of place for me to mention here, in passing, an opinion from the book of the elder Hippocrates <note>the famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>—or of another memorable man, as Galen <note>another influential ancient physician</note> would have it—concerning the *Sacred Disease* or the *Comitial Disease* <note>original: "Morbo sacro aut Comitiali" — so called because an epileptic seizure during a Roman public assembly (comitia) was seen as a bad omen that required the meeting to be dissolved</note>, which the Greeks call epilepsy. In this work, after he had first demonstrated that there is no more "divinity" in this evil than in any other diseases, he spoke as follows: 

"Those who first pronounced this disease to be 'sacred' seem to me to have been the same kind of men as those who exist even now: magicians <note>original: "magi"</note>, purifiers <note>original: "expiatores"</note>, charlatans <note>original: "circulatores" — literally "men who hang around in circles," referring to street performers or sellers of fake cures</note>, and certain arrogant men who pretend to be intensely pious and to know something more than others. Thus, these people—veiling and cloaking their own lack of judgment and mental poverty with the pretext of 'divinity'—pronounced this condition to be 'sacred' because they had nothing to offer that would actually help, and they did so to prevent their own ignorance from becoming obvious.

<margin>Against crafty physicians and sacrilegious magicians: the excellent opinion of Hippocrates.</margin>

And having gathered together plausible-sounding reasons, they established a method of treatment that was safe for themselves: they offered atonements <note>original: "expiamenta"</note> and incantations, and they commanded the patients to abstain from baths and from many foods unsuitable for sick people to eat, and so on. Furthermore, they commanded that a black cloak must not be worn, for the color black belongs to death. Nor should one cross one’s legs, nor one's hands, for they claimed all these things were impediments to the cure. They apply all these conditions under the guise of 'divinity,' as if they possessed some higher knowledge, and they put forward these pretexts so that if the patient should happen to recover, the glory and skill might be ascribed to them. But if the patient dies, their own reputations are placed in safety..." <note>The sentence continues on the next page, implying that if the patient dies, the practitioners blame the patient's failure to follow the superstitious rules rather than their own incompetence.</note>

...that swift rivers are turned back, the sluggish sea is bound, lifeless winds expire, the sun is inhibited, the moon is drawn down <note>original: "despumari" — literally "foamed down," a common poetic term in Latin for drawing down the moon through magic</note>, stars are plucked out, day is removed, and night is held fast.

<margin>The pact is an illusion.</margin>
I now proceed to the matter itself, namely the pact: it is easily recognized as illusory, brought about by a phantasm or imagination, or by the spirit's deceptive appearance in a spectral body. It is fashioned and stabilized by the spirit's art, either through a craftily implanted appearance in the optic or visual nerves—whatever appearance Satan desires—or by a whistling, whispering, or murmuring in the organs of hearing, corresponding to the images of a corrupted form. Consequently, it is of no weight or substance, especially if the differing essences of the contracting parties, the form of the contract, the manner, and the circumstances are inspected with a sharp mental gaze and weighed precisely in the balance of our reason and faith.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Thus it becomes clear that almost all the actions hitherto attributed to the <term>Lamia</term> <note>A term Weyer uses for a woman accused of witchcraft, derived from the mythological child-eating demon; he argues they are victims of delusion rather than practitioners of real magic.</note>—which she, being of unsound mind, also confesses to be her own—exist through a corrupted imaginative faculty. These actions belong not to the witch, but to Satan himself. He has no need for another’s assistance in displaying his power or carrying out his deeds. He is compelled by no one’s will or command except that of God and His good ministers. That ancient, wicked deceiver does not obey the wicked because he is forced, but does so willingly and indeed gladly, though he may feign and pretend otherwise—as Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on demons.</note> testifies—so that he may better entangle us in his illusions. Furthermore, it is not necessary for an imaginary pact, entered into deceitfully and falsely by the other party, to be strictly binding, since it is conducted by a deceptive spirit among...

<margin>If there is any power in the chrism, it cannot be removed by an external extraction.</margin>
If you take refuge in the idea that the <term>chrism</term> <note>Consecrated oil used in baptism and confirmation, symbolizing the Holy Spirit.</note> is removed or extracted during the contract of the [diabolical] covenant, I could satisfy this objection with a single word. However, lest it cause more trouble, it will be safer to respond thus: If there is any power in the chrism, it no more consists in the external smearing of oil than the power of the sacrament of **Baptism** consists in the external pouring of water. Baptism is sanctified through the intervention of faith and is so confirmed that even if the water poured on the body were washed away a hundred times—or indeed, if the entire skin were scraped off—the essence of baptism nevertheless remains because of the "character" <note>In Catholic theology, the "sacramental character" is an indelible spiritual mark on the soul that cannot be removed.</note> impressed by faith. Even if a person should at some time deny its power through a fall [into sin], yet if they rise again, converted from sins to the amendment of life through repentance, the power of the baptism once administered will still stand. 

The logic regarding the chrism will be the same for one who repents, if you will; otherwise, it would follow that the chrism would also perish if a wound were inflicted on the **forehead** <note>original: "synciput" — the crown or front of the head where the oil was applied during rites.</note> or if a rotting ulcer broke out in that spot. # On the Illusions of Demons

...in this situation: he attacks, pursues, and entices individuals in a specific manner, once he has learned the pursuits and emotions of each person’s mind through certain signs. Such is the nearly incomprehensible subtlety and tireless deception of these impure spirits, mocking the senses of men.

<header>Book Two</header>

Aristotle, in his book *On the Motion of Animals*, according to the common commentary in chapter 6, says: ***“Furthermore, imaginings <note>original: *phantasiæ*</note>, senses, and meditations can alter the body.”*** He continues: ***“Indeed, imagination and intelligence possess the power of actual things; for in a certain way, the mental image <note>original: *species intellecta*; in medieval philosophy, a 'species' was the form or likeness of an object perceived by the mind.</note> of heat or cold, or of something pleasant or sad, exists in the same way as the actual object itself.”*** Because of this, people tremble and feel fear just by thinking of such things. Add to this that mental images and imaginings remain even when the physical objects of the senses are absent, as Aristotle testifies in the second book of *On the Soul*; consequently, from the local movement of these sensory forms remaining within the power of the imagination—along with the humors <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, 'humors' were the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and emotion.</note> in which they reside as if in a container—certain things appear to us that do not actually exist. Similarly, in the book *On Sleep and Waking*, he says: *“When a great deal of blood descends to the sensory source, the forms conceived in the imagination descend along with it.” By this same reasoning, demons are able to move the humors of the internal and external senses, and thus bring certain images to the organs as if they were occurring from the outside, whether we are asleep or awake.*

<margin>
In the book *On the Divination of Demons*, chapters 3 and 5; also in the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 28.

Therefore, what **Boethius** <note>Hector Boece (c. 1465–1536), a Scottish philosopher and historian whose *Scotorum Historiae* often blended legendary tales with historical facts.</note> reports—as an author not unskilled in composing history in an agreeable manner—he wrote for the sake of attracting readers. His aim was that those who might not be delighted by **Scythian** <note>original: "Scythica." At the time, it was a common belief that the Scots were descended from the Scythians.</note> deeds and customs, nor by the description of the region, might at least have their boredom lessened by these fables. Nor is this a fault in a historian; indeed, where history is of itself sterile, it is permissible to adorn it with descriptions of places and stories. 

For this reason, **Titus Livy** <note>The famous Roman historian known for a more sober, factual style.</note> rightly abstained from such things; **Herodotus** <note>The Greek "Father of History," often criticized by later scholars for including fantastical "traveler's tales."</note> is justly condemned for them, and **Saxo Grammaticus** <note>A Danish historian (c. 1160–1220) known for including Norse myths in his chronicles.</note> is praised. But it is also most relevant that Boethius found these things already written, and the deed itself <note>The magical assassination attempt.</note> lies outside the bounds of traditional history. 

In the narration of history itself, however—such as the customs of the nation, wars, battles, the number of the slain, or the names of those who participated in battle or who bore themselves strenuously; the origins of families, the causes of wars, the calculation of dates, and the deeds and succession of princes, which are the "limbs" of which history consists—he was most diligent. 

Moreover, in those matters which pertain to history, nothing was so small that he neglected it, omitted it, or narrated it differently than it truly was. Such matters include the location and size of the region and its cities, the towns, islands, groves, mountains, new types of plants, four-legged animals, birds, serpents, fish, the fertility of the soil, the changing of the winds, the mildness of the climate, the lakes, marshes, distances, and all other rare things useful for understanding history. In such matters, he truly believed the history should be adorned, either because he believed them to be true, or perhaps because he was otherwise not initiated into the sacred rites of **philosophy** <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to natural philosophy or science, implying Boethius lacked the scientific training to see through the "supernatural" claims he recorded.</note>. Indeed, one part appeared pitch-black, but flecked with yellow drops, while the other part appeared whitish; for, according to the different species of the serpents, a double color had stained the porridge. When each of them had tasted only a small portion of it, Eric—judging the meal not by the appearance of the colors but by the effect of its internal power—quickly turned the platter and transferred the black part of the dish, which was prepared with the more potent juice, to himself. He moved the whitish part, which had been set before him, to Roller, thus conducting his dinner more successfully. And so that his industrious trickery might not be noticed, he said, "In this way, when the sea is surging, the stern is usually turned into the prow." Nor was the wit of the man thin, as he borrowed a disguise for his clever deed from the habits of navigation. And so Eric, now refreshed by the auspicious feast, attained the highest weight of human wisdom through its internal workings. Indeed, the vigor of the meal, beyond what could be believed, implanted in him such an abundance of all sciences that he was even skilled in the interpretation of the voices of wild animals and cattle. <meta>This page continues Johann Weyer’s medical and skeptical analysis of the "witches' ointments" mentioned on the previous page. ### On the Illusions of Demons

<margin>*A very sleep-inducing oil.*</margin>
To produce a deep and long sleep, I will add here a recipe for an oil. Take four ounces each of the seeds of darnel <note>original: "lolium"; a weed often infected with a fungus that causes drunkenness or hallucinations.</note>, henbane, hemlock, red and black poppy, lettuce, and purslane; and one ounce of the "inverse bean" <note>original: "faba inversa"; likely a reference to a specific legume used in early modern pharmacy, possibly the Orpine or a similar sedative plant.</note>. From all these, let an oil be made, and for every ounce of this oil, let two ounces of Thebaic opium <note>Opium from Thebes in Egypt, considered the highest quality in the Renaissance.</note> be mixed in. If two or three ounces of this are taken, a sleep of two days will follow.

<margin>*Simples that disturb and take away the senses.*</margin>
Certain <term>simples</term><note>In early medicine, "simples" were individual plant, animal, or mineral ingredients used on their own rather than in a compound mixture.</note> of this kind—such as darnel, the inverse bean, opium, henbane, hemlock, various species of poppy, <term>deadly nightshade</term><note>original: "solanum furiosum"; likely *Atropa belladonna*.</note>, and others of that genus—are well known to those skilled in natural things. By these substances, the intellect is either taken away or so disturbed that whoever uses them appears insane while speaking, hearing, and responding; or, they are plunged into a most profound sleep lasting for several days. However, I have preferred to wrap their use—and the methods for making waters, wines, powders, <term>troches</term><note>Small medicated lozenges.</note>, oils, and other forms from them—in silence, lest I seem to have provided anyone with an opportunity to abuse them. The most kind Author of all good <note>A reference to God.</note> has granted us a mind for the purpose of helping always, and never for doing harm.

<margin>*Frequent use of opium among the Turks and Persians.*</margin>
Here, in passing, because of its rarity and the near-miraculous nature of the matter, I should not overlook that the eating of opium is so familiar to the Turks, and even more so to the Persians, that almost nothing is more common. They are persuaded that by devouring it, they become stronger and fear the dangers of war less. In the same way, we observe in these regions that drunkards also cast themselves more fearlessly into any waves of shipwreck or danger. For this reason, whenever the Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan or military leadership.</note> gathers an army, the entire land is stripped of opium, although—

<meta>Catchword: although— (original: "cet quo-")</meta>

He also compares the use of opium for courage in the Ottoman Empire to the recklessness of drunkards in Europe.</summary>

Among the Greeks it is called *ephialtes* <note>original: "ἐφιάλτης"</note>, that is, "the leaper-upon," as if someone leaps on, applying force and compressing the person so they cannot move until they are freed from the invader. These signs arise from diminished heat: and when the **animal spirits** <note>In early medicine, these were "vapors" in the brain responsible for thought and movement.</note> existing in the brain are darkened by vapors rising from **phlegm** <term>pituita: the humor associated with coldness and moisture</term> and **melancholy** <term>black bile: the humor associated with coldness and dryness</term>, the mental faculty is oppressed, and it seems as if something heavy is being inflicted upon one, though in reality it is not. It happens most often when the body is lying on its back, usually when the opening of the stomach is oppressed either by thick and sticky phlegm or by a quantity of foods difficult to digest. 

Since, in truth, **witches** <term>sagae: a common term for wise-women or sorceresses, here used dismissively</term> are, on account of their sex, mostly phlegmatic, and on account of the passions of the mind, melancholic, why would they not be subject to this kind of illness when lying on their backs? # On the Delusions of Demons

<margin>A **priest** <note>original: "sacrificus"</note> suffering from an **Incubus**.</margin>

"Friend," he said, "unless you help a wretched and afflicted man, it is all over, and I am utterly lost: a wasting disease has seized me. Do you not see how emaciated I am, how bloodless, covered by barely a thin skin? I used to be full-fleshed, quite handsome, and in good condition; now I seem a foul **specter** <term>spectrum: a ghostly or terrifying apparition</term>, and the empty image of a man."

"What," I asked, "is tormenting you, and what do you think is the cause of your condition?"

"I will tell you," he said, "without fear, though you will be greatly amazed. Almost every night, a certain woman—not unknown to me—visits me and glides onto my chest; she forcefully compresses me and narrows the passages of my breath so that I can hardly breathe. Indeed, when I wish to cry out, she blocks the path of my voice, so that although I strive to lift myself up out of fear, I am entirely unable to do so. I cannot move my hands to repel the injury, nor my feet to take flight. She holds me bound and pinned down."

"Hey," I said, smiling, "you speak of nothing marvelous" (for I understood from his narration that it was an **incubus** <note>Weyer recognizes the priest's description as a classic case of sleep paralysis, which he treats as a medical condition rather than a supernatural one.</note>); "it is a mere **phantom** <note>original: "phantasma"</note>, a mere mockery."

Not pausing for more, he said, "A phantom? A mockery? It certainly is not! As God loves me, I am relating what I have seen with these very eyes and what I have felt with these very hands. Indeed, while awake and in full possession of my mind, I see her right in front of me and receive her as she attacks. I try to struggle, but because of my exhaustion, fear, distress, and the force applied, I achieve nothing. Driven mad by this matter, I have run here and there, asking anyone if they could help a man perishing miserably. I consulted a **Minorite** <term>Minoritam: a friar of the Franciscan Order</term>, whom they call a cunning old hand; from him, I was hoping for immediate aid..."
