# On the Delusions of Demons

In this way they corrupted their husbands: from which more corrupt children were born, the origin of evil, the mingling of godly blood with the ungodly. Therefore, those born were warlike, proud, and insolent. These things are more true and not inconsistent with nature; whereas those other stories are no different from the fables of poets. It is neither possible by nature, nor does philosophy agree, that spirits stripped of bodies could be seized by the love of women, or be able to procreate from them. 

For desires have their own source and lower origins: if the cause is lacking, the effect is lacking. Where there are no genital members, there is no love of copulation. Where there is no food and drink, there is no semen. Where succession and propagation were not sought, nature did not apply the desire for procreation. Just as naked spirits cannot thirst or hunger, so they cannot be inflamed by the lust of Venus <note>original: "ueneris libidine" — a reference to sexual desire or passion.</note>. It is also absurd that there should be two kinds of demons: both the angels themselves fallen into concupiscence, and the souls of the Giants. 

For the Giants were men, nor should demons be made out of men; nor was their fall because they burned with love. Therefore, these demons would be mythical <note>original: "fabulosi"</note>, both those whom lust supposedly seized, and those generated from them. They would be like Hector, Achilles, Aeneas, and Hercules—born from humans and gods in the works of poets. *These are the words of Agostino Steuco* <note>Agostino Steuco (1497–1548) was a prominent Italian humanist scholar and theologian whom Weyer uses here as a prestigious authority to debunk the physical reality of incubi.</note>. The demons lie about being captured by love, so that they may in turn bind these mindless women more tightly in their service, ardently longing for the destruction of souls.

As for the particular fiction devised about the demon’s intercourse first with a man, and then with a woman... <note>Weyer is beginning to address the "Succubus/Incubus" theory, where a demon was thought to steal semen as a woman and deliver it as a man.</note>

This only will I say: that particular balance of semen, composed of blood and vital spirit and fit for generation in the organs ordained by God, is corrupted and dies if it is removed from its own proper vessels, especially through any kind of transfer. Nor should we believe the commentator of **Albertus Magnus** <note>original: "Alberti ſcholiaſtæ"</note> here, who reports as if in a dream that if semen emitted onto the ground were placed near the womb, it would be possible for it to conceive. For by this logic, if a cat were to pour its semen over sage, and someone were to eat this sage, then cats would be generated from that semen in the man’s stomach, only to be expelled by vomiting. These things are too absurd and false to require a longer refutation.

<margin>The Satyr Islands. Satyrs.</margin>
Concerning those lustful Satyrs who are also thrust upon us <note>i.e., presented as evidence for demonic activity</note>, and who are held in the same category as Sylvans and Fauns <note>Woodland deities from Roman myth often associated with unbridled nature and sexuality</note>—as to whether they were true demons, I will briefly add what Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> wrote in his *Description of Attica* <note>original: "in Atticis"</note>. "Indeed," he says, "wishing to know something more certain than what has been handed down by others regarding who the Satyrs are, I inquired into many individual accounts. Euphemus the Carian, a man of no small reputation, recounted these things to me: that while he was sailing to Italy, he was carried by the force of the winds to the farthest edges of the Ocean. There, he said, are many desert islands inhabited by wild men. The sailors were unwilling to land at the other islands because they were not ignorant of the inhabitants who held them, having landed there before; but then, even against their will, they were driven there by a storm. These islands are called the 'Satyrides' by the sailors. The inhabitants are reddish-skinned <note>original: "russos"</note> and have tails on their lower backs not much smaller than those of horses. As soon as they sensed the visitors, they rushed to the ship without making a sound and laid hands on the women who were on board. The terrified sailors set a barbarian woman out on the island; the Satyrs rushed upon her and most shamelessly assaulted not only that part which nature exposed to men, but any other part as well."

But this man [Pico della Mirandola]—otherwise not unwise, yet too addicted to the figments of certain Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who often believed in intermediary spirits or demons existing between the human and divine realms.</note>—has mixed the lies of monks, the rumors of the common people, and the trifles and tales of old women worthy of the *Golden Ass* <note>A famous ancient Roman novel by Apuleius involving magic and transformations; here used as a synonym for ridiculous fiction.</note>, with the sacred discourses of philosophy. He has most foully defiled the whole art, being neither a Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy, which generally emphasized empirical observation and logic.</note> in any sense, nor sufficiently a Christian in this regard, nor even agreeing with the tenets of the famous Platonists, among whose flock he considered himself to be one. 

Thus it happened that he seemed more to delight and entice his readers than to treat anything seriously. But even the blessed Augustine, if he had abstained from such absurd narratives, might perhaps have had fewer readers, yet he would have attained the reputation of a more serious man among the learned. But such was the decay of that age that many competed with grander lies—just as they now do regarding the affairs of kingdoms—which that holy man, accepting as true and as if in emulation of the fictions of the pagans, inserted into his books. Therefore, I place only as much faith in him as...

...as much as he testified that he saw with his own eyes; in other matters, not at all. For it is now evident to everyone that the greater part of such narratives is fictional. # On the Illusions of Demons

...[mid]dle, in the most foul business of this mocking intercourse <note>original: *commixtionis*; referring to the alleged sexual union between witches and demons</note>, so that since that entire crowd of witches <note>original: *sagarum*</note> confesses to being defiled by it, and each one points out her suitor <note>original: *procum*</note> by a specific name, if I can establish that there is no truth in this meeting, that whole engine of demonic phantasms might more readily collapse, the truth might shine more brightly, the devil's kingdom might sink deeper into ruin, and unity among the Christian people might be reborn sooner and preserved more inviolably.

Furthermore, to finally begin bringing this act of the story <note>original: *fabulae*</note> to a close: just as these witches <term>lamiae|Weyer uses this term for women accused of witchcraft, whom he believes are suffering from mental illness or demonic delusion rather than actual magical power</term> do not seek out the doctrine of a corrupted mind alongside more wicked people through long travels, labor, or study; so too they have no books by whose assistance they might be trained or advanced in their profession. They have no prescribed formulas of conjuration that they follow. Moreover, they do not carry around any demon imprisoned in a ring or enclosed within the solidness of a crystal for their service, as many mages <term>magi|Weyer distinguishes between the "magi"—learned men who perform ritual magic—and the "lamiae," who are usually poor, uneducated women</term> do. 

<margin>The teacher of the witches: a corrupted imagination.</margin>

They venerate and worship only an imagination <note>original: *phantasiam*</note> corrupted by various images forced upon it by an unclean spirit. Trusting in this far too readily, they are miserably deceived and rush toward their own destruction. Nor can they do anything unusual beyond the ordinary course of things, owing to the dullness of their nature and the unsuitability of their spirits—even though such a thing would be very easy for a demon due to its thinness and subtlety. And if I may maintain this point: nowhere in the entire Holy Bible is there any mention made of the witches we have discussed...

Furthermore, I have already demonstrated that such sorcery has no power in itself; since, however, some harm seems to follow from it, it remains that this is stirred up by Satan himself, with God's permission, on account of a person's lack of faith <note>original: *incredulitatem*; here implying a failure to trust in divine protection</note>, or even so that the person might be tested just as Job was. Meanwhile, the devil firmly suggests and persuades the mind of this old woman—who has buried poisonous material or some other kind—that what was actually perpetrated by him, or happened by chance, was done by her, so that she believes and asserts it to be her doing.

Some people later attempted the same thing in Geneva, and they paid the penalty. It is also certain that others in Milan smeared the door bars; but when they were subjected to interrogation <term>quaestionibus|formal judicial examination, which in this period almost certainly included the use of torture</term>, they confessed nothing, and since no one had died, they were released. Bassianus Landus <note>a 16th-century Italian physician known for his writings on anatomy and the plague</note> writes that in Padua, a certain monk repeatedly conspired with many others who, during a time of plague, secretly threw infected linens into houses so that the contagion would spread to many people; they also suffered the ultimate punishment.

*In the noble Petrini family of Bologna, there were two brothers, one of whom was a husband living in the same house with his numerous children and his widowed mother. The other brother, however, being younger, decided to do away with the entire family in the hope of obtaining the whole inheritance, by throwing arsenic into a wine cask. When they were tormented by severe symptoms from its use, all the most celebrated doctors were summoned: Matteo Corti <note>Mattheus Curtius (1475–1544), one of the most famous medical professors of the Renaissance</note>, Giovanni Maria Betti, and the Spaniard Philippaldus. They soon suspected poison because they understood that neighbors who had happened to enter the house and drank that wine were also afflicted with the same agonies. Therefore, by their advice, the vessel was broken open, and once the wine was poured out, arsenic was found. The doctors then undertook the treatment and restored everyone to health, except for the mother, a weak old woman, and a sickly boy. The poisoner <term>veneficus|literally "one who uses poisons," but often carries the dual meaning of a sorcerer or witch</term> looked to his safety by fleeing, and in this way, the author of the poisoning became known. This crime occurred in the year one thousand five hundred and thirty-eight, in August.*

<margin>Helidæus Paduanus of Forlì, physician.</margin>
Furthermore, in Bologna, a certain son-in-law offered his mother-in-law cantharides <term>cantharides|also known as "Spanish fly," a highly toxic powder made from dried beetles; though used as an aphrodisiac, it is a dangerous irritant to the urinary tract</term> mixed with cassia <note>original: "cassiæ," a plant pulp used in the period as a mild laxative</note>. This was recounted by Master Johann Ewich <note>Johannes Echtivs (1515–1566), a physician from Cologne and student of the famous doctors of his day</note>, a most distinguished physician who was formerly his student, who followed him at that time and was also present at the previous cure. To this same man, Master Gisbert Horstius, a most experienced physician, had also narrated that in Rome, a certain man with dropsy <term>hydropicum|a condition now known as edema, involving the painful accumulation of fluids in the body's tissues</term> had been bedridden for a long time. His wife, finally weary of the expenses of his care, decided to kill him with poison. For this reason, she gave the patient the powder of a toad burned in a pot to drink; from this, he passed a copious amount of urine. Because of this, she administered the same powder again, so that he might more quickly exchange his miserable and costly life for a sudden death; however, having been unburdened of a much more plentiful watery ballast <note>original: "saburra aquea," a metaphorical description of the fluid buildup in dropsy</note>, he recovered, contrary to his wife’s expectation. Gisbert himself elsewhere experienced a similar calamity from those by whom it was least fitting.

...near the Meuse, located on the borders of Brabant, in a place called Grave, my own birthplace. When three out of five captives were to be punished on the same day for their shameful crimes, an executioner <note>original: "carnifex"</note> was summoned from the nearby city of Nijmegen in Guelders. He followed the summons, hoping they were to be hanged according to the decree of the magistrate; however, when he understood that the sentence pronounced was the punishment of beheading, he complained of his own weakness to the governor <term>satrapam|a term for a high-ranking official or provincial governor</term> Steinhusius. He had contracted this infirmity a year earlier from poison secretly administered to him by his own servant, so that the servant might be substituted into his master’s service (such is the envy that usually exists regarding high positions and distinguished offices). 

Lest the execution be delayed any longer, he promised that he would immediately send word to his wife, who would call his colleague from Arnhem to carry out the sentence that had been passed. For he asserted that he had an agreement with that colleague for mutual work and shared profit—as is often the case among faithful craftsmen, that an equal gain returns from a pact. The prefect consented, and a messenger was sent to Nijmegen to the executioner’s wife, so that the public official of that same office might be summoned from Arnhem immediately. 

She, however, being greedy for profit, decided on another plan in her mind: namely, to supply her husband's deficiency with her own strength. Therefore, she obtained for her husband the sword destined for that final tragic act, and soon brought it to a bladesmith to be sharpened on the right side; for she herself was left-handed <note>original: "sinistra erat," implying she needed the blade's edge adjusted for her dominant hand</note>. Then, in the evening hour, she ordered her hair to be secretly cut, and very early in the morning, dressed in her husband's clothes, with a feathered hat placed on her head, and that broad sword...

However, having returned to Nijmegen, she was celebrated with laughter among many, as if made famous by such a bold deed.

Hence, **on the authority of Pausanias and Aelian**, Phormis of Arcadia <note>A celebrated ancient soldier and benefactor at Olympia.</note> recognized such great power in this substance that he placed a bronze horse at Olympia, made of a mixture of copper and tin, with its tail cut off. Into this statue, he had enclosed *hippomanes*. The craftsmanship was not so accurate that the horses should have been driven into such a frenzy at the sight of it through visual deception alone; yet it attracted them so strongly and agitated them with such madness that, having broken their reins, they would leap upon the statue more violently than upon a living mare. Nor did their desire cease because their hooves, clinging to the bronze statue, would slip off its smooth surface; rather, they would whinny before it much more ardently. They could not be driven away from the bronze image until they were dragged off by whips and the violence of the grooms. There is also a type of *hippomanes*, as Theocritus <note>An ancient Greek poet.</note> teaches, which is a <term>plant of horses</term> <note>original Greek: "φυτὸν ἵππων"</note>—that is, a plant or herb which, when tasted, drives horses into a frenzy; hence its name.

<margin>Love poisons.</margin>
Among these love poisons <note>original: "amatoria venena"</note> are also numbered: a hair from the tip of a wolf's tail and the wolf's penis, the small *remora* fish <note>A fish traditionally believed to be able to stop ships by clinging to them.</note>, the brains of a cat and a lizard, and the lizard named the *stincus* <note>Likely the "skink" (Scincus scincus), often used in historical pharmacy.</note>. It is also claimed to be useful if someone looks at a woman while a hyena's uterus is bound to their left arm. These potions are also sometimes composed of excrement, or animals born from rot, or from matter produced by our own bodies. These substances, however—rightly considered illicit—disturb and change the mind rather than compel one to love. # Book Two

...[the drink], so greatly fascinates and infects those drinking it that it renders them moon-struck and insane. Other love potions <note>original: "philtra"</note> are also kept, taken from the clothes of the dead, candles, measures, needles, and generally from those things prepared for the sake of funerals; these I mention all the more willingly because they contain more nonsense than truth. In the same way, I have preferred to bury in silence here those natural and excessively effective poisons, which are sufficiently known to more learned doctors from the sixth book of Dioscorides’ <term>materia medica</term> <note>A foundational ancient Greek encyclopedia of herbal medicine and related substances.</note>, and from the remaining books of the Greeks and Arabs, as well as from the works of certain more recent authors and from daily practice.

<margin>Sorceries destroy living creatures.</margin>
Furthermore, sorcerers harm and kill living creatures by poisons <note>original: "pharmacis"</note> cast into their fodder, or scattered in places to be tasted, or drawn in through the breath. While I do not deny that the same can be achieved by rubbing or application, one must also remember that some people intentionally hide wolf dung secretly in stables. When the livestock notice this by smell, fearing their voracious enemy due to a certain <term>antipathy</term> <note>A natural or occult aversion between certain animals or substances, a popular concept in early modern science.</note>, they are agitated by a wonderful frenzy. Thus, the ignorant—seeking counsel from the practitioners of this very art—firmly believe that the animals are being tormented by a magic spell. For the same reason, they say that a wolf’s tail suspended in a manger for oxen or horses terrifies them from eating. For, struck by fear because of the scent, they forget their food even while hungry; just as we experience happening to humans as well in times of great fear. It is not our intention to pursue natural poisons more extensively, since the thread of this discourse aims at this point: that actions and diseases striking beyond the laws of nature may be uncovered.

<summary>The author dismisses superstitious charms in favor of natural explanations, noting how natural substances like wolf dung can cause animal behaviors often misattributed to sorcery.</summary>

# BOOK III: CONCERNING THOSE WHO ARE THOUGHT TO BE AFFLICTED BY THE EVIL MAGIC OF WITCHES.

<margin>Who are those afflicted by harmful magic.</margin>
Those are said to be afflicted by harmful magic <note>original: "maleficio affecti"</note> who are tormented in their bodies by a demon in various and usually unusual ways, beyond the laws of nature, yet with God’s permission—whether they be humans or beasts. This happens when the demon either enters into them or remains outside, and either agitates and infects the beneficial <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) were thought to control health and temperament.</note> of the body, or transfers harmful ones into the vital organs <note>original: "partes principes"</note>. He may also obstruct the veins and natural channels, or dislocate the structure of the limbs, or disturb the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>Subtle substances thought to flow through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> and imbue them with manifold forms. Whether he defiles and disfigures them from within or without with poisonous matter or breath, or other such means, these causes give rise to innumerable, serious, and remarkable diseases. Nor, in the meantime, do the substance and faculties of men remain immune and free from the harmful magic of this subtle and crafty enemy.

<margin>Job 1. Job afflicted by harmful magic.</margin>
We see an example clearer than the midday sun in Job. By the effort of the devil, first fifty yoke of oxen <note>The Latin text here reads "quinquaginta" (50), though the Vulgate Bible usually lists five hundred.</note> and five hundred female donkeys are snatched away, and the servants are slain; secondly, seven thousand sheep along with the servants are consumed by fire sent down from heaven; thirdly, three thousand camels are led away, and the attendants perish; fourthly, the house—on account of the most violent storms stirred up by Satan—is torn from its very foundations and crushed in ruin.

<margin>Job 2.</margin>

<margin>Nebuchadnezzar harmed by evil magic. Daniel 4.</margin>

### Book Three.

Did not the woman who had a spirit of infirmity—as mentioned in <margin>*Luke 13*</margin>—bound by Satan for eighteen years and so bent over that she could not raise her head at all, experience things equal to those in our day who are believed to suffer from <term>harmful magic</term> <note>original: "maleficium"; a term usually implying a spell cast by a person, but Weyer argues it is often direct demonic work.</note>, until she was released from that bond by Christ on the Sabbath day? Who, unless they have a completely stubborn mind, would dare to deny that if those whom I have enumerated were seen in our own time, almost everyone would cry out with one voice that they were being tossed about against nature in various ways, miserably driven mad, crippled, tormented, and pulled apart by the craft of some wicked old woman? 

And yet, by whose art does Scripture testify that they were oppressed by this dreadful calamity? By the demon’s. By whose cooperation or command? By no one's, but only by the malice of the demons' own will and by God’s permission from His secret counsel, so that they might be either tested, punished, or corrected. Nor will you find anywhere in the vast volume of the Old and New Testaments an example where Satan used, or even required, the help of any <term>witch</term> <note>original: "Lamia"; Weyer uses this term to refer to the stereotypical "night-witch" of folklore.</note> in afflicting bodies; yet it must be admitted that nothing has been omitted there that could show his power, actions, and deceptions.

I also thought that this should by no means be passed over in silence: that this girl never spat out those rags, threads, pins, needles, or keys from her mouth until she was first taken to Amersfoort <note>A city in the Netherlands</note> on account of some pain or other. This occurred because of unbelief—because the pain, which arose from a natural cause by the hidden will of God, was not recognized as such, but was instead attributed to a "witch," and recourse was had to illicit counsels.

"On other occasions," he says, "I have often seen that those infected by the aforementioned <term>maleficium</term> <note>harmful magic or a curse</note>, when they employed a remedy for their liberation, would frequently vomit from their mouths or discharge through their bowels needles, hair, iron tools, nails, feathers, sulfur, stones, and finally such things that it would have been impossible for the victim to have swallowed—not only as whole objects, but not even if they had been broken or cut into tiny pieces."

Wherefore this seems a thing to be wondered at; but consider, as some have judged, that Satan—to better deceive mankind—causes these strange appearances to be seen during the resolution of the <term>factura</term> <note>original: *facturæ*; in demonology, this refers to the physical object or "make" used to cast a spell</note>, so that the event appears even more miraculous. But in truth, these are not natural objects. That this is the case is apparent from this fact: although they are ejected through vomiting or the bowels, and thus appear among those liquid substances when they are first emitted from the body, if you keep those materials for two or three days, or even five—just as I once carefully had them kept—you will see that all of them have completely liquefied, and their forms have entirely vanished. <margin>Hard matter ejected by vomiting liquefies.</margin> If they were natural things, they would surely remain in their prior or original form, and they could not be destroyed by any liquids or moisture, [as he] knows.

# On the Deceptions of Demons

...especially iron and stones, because of their natural hardness: as is clear to everyone. Some others have said that demons—so that the thing might seem marvelous—at the time when the victim affected by the <term>maleficium</term> <note>harmful magic or a curse</note> is moved to vomit or to the work of the bowels, very swiftly and invisibly bring there those shapes or materials mentioned above. But note: although a demon, by his natural power, could indeed do this and insert them in such a dexterous manner during the vomiting or the excrement of the one suffering the curse that no man would notice, the former opinion nevertheless pleases me more: namely, that they are apparent shapes appearing under those forms, and are not natural. 

That this is true is apparent from the reason mentioned before: because they generally do not last in that form, but in a short time are dissolved into those liquids with which they had emerged mixed. As I have frequently seen and handled with my own hands, things which at the beginning (as I said) appeared true and natural and held in themselves a certain hardness; yet in a short time, as stated, they were dissolved and perished. *It is beyond belief, what we ourselves saw when we were in Crete. A peasant was wounded in a riotous mob by an arrow struck into his back. For the sake of the miracle, it was shown to be of a barbed shape, two fingers wide. For first it penetrated the diaphragm with its point, where the fleshier part is; then, having slipped down along the intestines, it gradually cut through the anus <term>podicem</term> near the belly.*

...cut, and made a path for itself toward an exit while partially corroded; regarding which there was a great dispute among physicians. The same author, in Book 2, Chapter 9 of his *Anatomy* <margin>Chapter 9.</margin>, writes: Those who think that the openings of the mesenteric veins <term>venae mesenteriacae</term> <note>The veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver.</note> among the intestines are larger in a living person but shrink away in a corpse are greatly deceived. For they believe that fragments of food can be drawn through these very thin fibers; and they think that a young woman in Venice in our time, while we were writing this, who had held a hair-pin <note>original: *crinalem acum*</note> four fingers long between her teeth as she was about to sleep and inadvertently swallowed it in her sleep <margin>A needle swallowed, expelled with the urine.</margin>, passed it through her urine after ten months with the greatest agony. This happened because viscous humors <note>In the medical theory of the time, "humors" were bodily fluids; an excess of thick or "viscous" fluid was thought to harden into stones.</note> collected in the bladder, and a stone <term>calculus</term> had formed around the needle to the size of a hen's egg. They contend that the needle was first sucked up by the mesenteric veins.

I will add here in passing that the example of that needle returned through the urine has disturbed many who are ignorant of dissection <note>Weyer refers to those who do not understand internal anatomy through the practice of autopsy or surgery.</note>. They falsely believe that it penetrated through the mesenteric veins <term>venae mesaraicae</term> from the stomach to the liver, and through the larger vein <note>Likely the vena cava.</note> to the narrow passages of the kidneys, and from there to the bladder, thinking the mouths of the fibers are more open in living people to receive the needle. However, the needle, by its own sharp point, gradually and over a long time penetrated through the intestines (since whatever is propelled by nature makes a path for itself). From there, it passed through the fleshy part of the bladder, and then could be expelled through the urinary passage. In the same manner, we should consider the case of an iron arrowhead, which by the guidance of nature cut through the appropriate parts over two years; a fact I could easily prove with other wonderful examples.

Whether this seems plausible <note>The OCR reads "numerifimile," likely a typo for "verisimile" (plausible).</note> is for others to judge. However, I am not unaware that monstrous worms are sometimes born within the human organs from natural causes. There was also a false suspicion spread regarding a certain girl, that a serpent was dwelling in her stomach, causing her torments and occasionally climbing up toward her throat; she was under my care, and she is now doing well <note>Weyer frequently treated patients whose "supernatural" ailments turned out to be physical or psychological.</note>.

<margin>How a ball in an ox's stomach is formed.</margin>
For several years, I kept a large ball, about the size of a large fist, perfectly spherical without a seam, and very tightly packed with small, soft hairs. It had been removed from the stomach of a healthy young ox that had been sent to the slaughterhouse. Many would exclaim that this object had been placed there by an incantation <note>Weyer is referring to the common folk belief that finding a "bezoar" or hairball in an animal was a sign of a curse or "hex-food" (Maleficium).</note>; however, I wish to investigate the natural cause of how this ball was generated.

Calves that are still living on their mother’s milk, if they are ever lacking food, or are otherwise becoming unruly at a frisky age, will run to their mother or to another cow. They greedily suck on the cow’s calves <note>The lower legs of the cow.</note> or whatever hairy spot they can reach with their mouths—especially the back of the haunches—sucking so vigorously that they even make the area bald. These hairs are drawn into the stomach by the strong and frequent suction. Through the animal's constant movement and playful jumping, the hairs are gradually clumped together. They are usually enveloped in chyle <term>chylus</term> <note>The milky fluid consisting of lymph and emulsified fats, formed in the small intestine during digestion.</note> or a slow, phlegmatic juice. Over time, this juice becomes more tenacious and takes on the appearance of a membrane. Indeed, when this ball was first seen immediately after the animal was cut open, its outer skin appeared as a slimy, whitish substance. Later, as it gradually dried, it took on the appearance of even dyed leather...

Thus it happens that later, when he has driven people to forbidden counsels and made them guilty of impiety, he willingly ceases from his work, not being forced in the least—even though he may pretend to be compelled <note>Demonologists often argued that demons only left when "forced" by exorcists, but Weyer argues they leave voluntarily to trick people into believing in the efficacy of superstitious rituals.</note>, so that he may confirm some superstition or other and ensnare others more tightly. 

For if these members <note>Weyer is referring to the "theft" of male genitals, a common claim in the witch-hunting manual *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> were truly taken away, when was this done, and by what means? Could such a thing be done without the shedding of blood, without injury or wounding of the parts, with all sensation removed, and then healed in a single moment? And even if we grant this, though it is <term>impossible</term> <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton); a Greek term meaning something physically or logically impossible.</note>: how, I ask, did the restoration occur if those parts, having been torn from the body and thus deprived of nourishment and the <term>vital spark</term> <note>original: "vitali fomite"; the internal heat or "tinder" believed to sustain life in the limbs.</note>, were dead and prone to decay for so long? Is it in the power of Satan and his angels to create new things? Or can they, by their own will, restore life to parts completely removed and lacking vital power, joining them back as if they were glued, or fixing them in their original place by their own power—just as we believe without doubt that the ear of Malchus, which was cut off by Peter, was restored by Christ? Not in the least. We have heard before that the demon is clearly able to create nothing; and it has been explained what is <term>inimitable</term> <note>original: "ἀμίμητον" (amimeton); things that cannot be imitated by demonic power.</note> to him.

Therefore, that defect should not always be attributed to an incantation, nor should an innocent person be immediately burdened with suspicion. I admit that the instruments of generation can indeed be rendered unfit for cohabitation by a demon; however, I steadfastly deny that this is effected by the malignant will and foolish imprecation of a most filthy old woman—even though she, led by the wicked persuasion of the demon, may sometimes believe otherwise.

# On the Illusions of Demons

<margin>Humans are not transformed into beasts by sorcery.</margin>
The credulous and superstitious ancients maintained that many people were turned into beasts by the <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "maleficio"</note> of witches. Thus <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist and author</note> also records <term>Demarchus</term> <note>Demarchus of Parrhasia, an Olympic athlete said to have been transformed into a wolf for nine years after a ritual sacrifice</note>, who, after tasting the entrails of a boy sacrificed in an offering, turned himself into a wolf (and a wolf may rightly be called "voracious" if he devours human entrails). It is also said that <term>Circe</term> <note>The mythological enchantress from Homer's Odyssey</note> changed the companions of <term>Ulysses</term> <note>The Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note> into wild beasts with her cup during that long wandering, as it appears in <term>Virgil</term> <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), the great Roman poet</note>:

> Whom the cruel goddess Circe, with her powerful herbs, 
> Had stripped of their human faces and clothed in the features and hides of wild beasts. 

Likewise in his *Eclogue 8*:

> By these I have often seen Moeris become a wolf and hide in the woods, 
> Often summon spirits from the depths of their graves, 
> And move standing crops from one field to another.

Weyer describes a physical stopper or plug inserted into the rectum to prevent the mercury from passing through too quickly.</note> deep into his fundament, and having swallowed a great deal of butter at the same time—with which the stomach and intestines were previously smeared and protected against the destructive force of **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyri deletoriã." Mercury was known to be toxic, but its high density and fluidity made it perfect for this deception.</note>—he would swallow **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver</term> <note>The liquid metal mercury.</note>. By its own weight, this was carried from the stomach through the **pylorus** <note>The opening from the stomach into the small intestine.</note> into the intestines. There, because of the plug placed at the opening, the way of exit was cut off. 

<margin>Mercury is extremely fluid and made of fine particles.</margin>

Therefore, since it is vehemently fluid, composed of very fine particles, and most restless with an innate mobility, although it was stirred by natural heat, it could not evaporate (even if the heat had been that intense) because of the windings of the intestines joined with butter. From this was stirred that powerful disturbance of the belly and unequal tossing, while the internal parts remained uninjured in the meantime because of the antidote of butter taken beforehand. Then, after the alms had been collected and the witnesses sent away, he would free the restless demon—that is, the captive **Mercury** <note>Weyer uses "Mercurius" as a pun, referring both to the Roman god and the metal.</note>—by pulling out the plug. 

I saw this actor ten days after this spectacle was performed; because of his robbery, he was subjected to the **German punishment of the wheel** <note>original: "Germanica punitione imponirotæ." Breaking on the wheel was a common and brutal form of capital punishment in early modern Europe.</note>. He came down from it two hours later, but was put back on the same day and strangled.

# On the Tricks of Demons

...lage <note>original: "vico-ge" - this completes the word from the previous page, referring to a village near Weimar.</note>, situated half a mile from Weimar <note>A city in Thuringia, Germany, known in the 16th century for its judicial proceedings.</note> of the Thuringians. Here, a cowherd by profession, having wandered for three years through several famous cities of Germany, pretended that on the very feast day of St. John <note>June 24th, a day often associated with folk magic and supernatural events in European tradition.</note> in the morning hours, while he was tending the oxen, he was enchanted by Nicolaus Gottel—who was afterwards burned at Weimar for his crimes—by taking a piece of **blue bread** <note>original: "pane assumpto cyaneo." Blue bread is a recurring motif in stories of diabolical pacts or charms in German folklore.</note> made from six kinds of blood (namely, of an infant not yet initiated by baptism, and of a snake, a toad, a hedgehog, a fox, and a wolf killed by him), so that for twelve years he might be fiercely tormented by the devil.

He asserted that Nicolaus had confessed this in prison. From this, he said the demon tortured him in many ways, and often tied his hands behind his back so tightly in an instant with bonds of horsehair and twisted silk scraps, that unless they were soon loosened by cutting, an eruption of blood would follow. For the inextricable knot of the binding was tightened by a singular artifice.

And before this, he complained that blood frequently flowed from his left ear and mouth due to his anguish; and among other things, he told that once at Mansfeld he was carried into the air, and by a strong wind transported beyond the walls of Halle <note>A significant city in Saxony-Anhalt.</note>, and there bound with silver chains. Likewise at Borna, where he had been shut in a tower so that he might be somewhat relieved from the devil's tortures and kept safe from his snares, he claimed he had been pulled out by the demon through a narrow opening in a thick vault <note>original: "foramen angustū crassi fornicis." This describes a miraculous or impossible escape through a solid stone ceiling.</note> broken by the devil, covered only in his shirt, and led into a vast wilderness; but how, he did not know; and there for three nights he [spent time] without any human food...

# On the Deceptions of Demons

...the other set out. By his dreadful exorcisms, the priest <note>original: "sacrificus"; Weyer often uses this term mockingly for a mass-priest or monk.</note> attempted to extort everything from the demon through interrogation, especially since he desired a particular vengeance and the slander of others. To these questions, the demon responded exactly as desired, having been coached beforehand. Among other things, the man asked what the cursed Satan felt was most hostile to him of all things. The "demon," having first hemmed and hawed for a while, finally said—as if forced—"Holy water." Then, with a resistant grunting, the priest poured in that sort of water as if it were the most contrary thing possible. He also applied to her neck, as a most powerful antidote <term>alexiterium: a medicine or charm intended to ward off poison or evil</term> against the violence of Satan, the relics of **Saint Gudula** <note>The patron saint of Brussels, whose relics were highly venerated in the Low Countries.</note> stored in a gilded casket. Whereupon, with her neck wonderfully swollen by a clever trick, she pretended to be severely tormented, crying out with a horrific voice like a pig that feels the butcher's hand cutting its throat. It also happened that the little priest urged the fabricated demon with dire execrations to depart. Finally, according to his own unique brand of learning, he cried: "He is outside!" <note>original: "Ipse est extrà"; Weyer is mocking the monk's poor Latin and clumsy performance.</note> However, when both of them returned to their true characters and persisted in their wicked deceit, the trickery was discovered some months later. I learned these things from the report of a learned and pious man, most worthy of trust, who was a spectator of this play.

<margin>Those infected by poisoning.</margin>
Furthermore, if any persons have been infected by poisoners—whether by poison offered to them, or smeared upon them, or by inhaling its vapor—the judgment should remain in the hands of physicians. It is the physicians who must distinguish here between poisons (whose hidden and lurking power wears a person down with various torments of symptoms) and the diseases born from them (which differ not only in their manifest qualities, but in the disposition of their entire substance)...

# Book Three

[per]fidy, it is established that the very beginnings of our life are demolished <note>original: "fidio, uitae nostrae primordia demoliri constat"; likely continuing from "perfidio" on the previous page.</note>); and among other common, rare, hidden, yet natural diseases, they will discern [these conditions] according to the peculiar marks of each.

<margin>Dioscorides, book 6, in the Preface.</margin>

Indeed, those who have been poisoned are affected in many different ways, depending on either the manifest qualities of the drug swallowed or applied, or by the hidden property of the entire substance. They may be heavily tried by torments of the stomach, the belly, the intestines, the liver, the kidneys, and the bladder; they may hiccup, have their insides eroded, tremble, grow cold, lose their speech, or be seized by convulsions. Their pulse may become difficult, a deep lethargy <term>ueternus: a heavy, morbid sleepiness or a comatose state</term> may weigh upon them, vertigo may spin before them, their senses may dim, and blood may burst forth. Likewise, they may be suffocated, or struggle with thirst or fever; they may pass urine with difficulty, be vexed by griping pains <note>original: "torminibus"; refers to acute colicky pains in the bowels.</note>, be oppressed by nausea, and vomit frequently. They may feel frequent fainting fits from excessive distress of the heart, grow weak with dysentery, turn red, rot with wasting disease, be marked by livid bruises, turn pale, rave, snore, or fail in their strength.

Indeed, from the bite of a **tarantula**, some laugh perpetually, others weep, others shout, others sleep, while others are afflicted by sleeplessness. Vomiting twists many; some dance; there are those who sweat, others who become trembling, and some who are haunted by terrors. Others suffer other inconveniences and are likened to the phrenetic <term>phreneticis: those suffering from "phrenitis," an acute fever with delirium</term>, the lymphatic <term>lymphaticis: historically, those driven mad by "nymphs"; here meaning a state of frantic delusion</term>, and the maniacal. And it is a marvel that, dancing continually upon hearing musical instruments, they are freed—once the force of the poison is imperceptibly dispersed through the pores of the skin and through sweat.

Poisons, however, and their signs, both general and specific, [were treated] no less diligently and...

# On the Delusions of Demons

<page-num>330</page-num>

<margin>Book 6 of *On Medical Matters*.</margin>
...[as] Dioscorides described [these things] with as much precision as he did learning; nor was the most diligent investigator of "simples" <term>medicinal plants or basic drugs</term>, Mattioli, slow to lend his efforts to explaining and adorning that work. 

<margin>
Poisons taken internally.
Those harming by contact.
</margin>
Among those substances taken internally, they cause harm far more instantly and violently than those that strike by contact. However, those that harm by contact are duller and less effective; they do not gain their power in the spirit or the air alone, but rather in some promoting moisture.

<margin>Those striking by breath.</margin>
Furthermore, the poison that strikes through the breath <note>original: "halitu"; refers to vapors, miasmas, or exhaled air</note> is the most immediate and effective of all; it requires neither moisture nor any thicker matter as a "vehicle" to act upon us or migrate into our systems. Indeed, since it is extremely thin, once it is drawn in by the breath, it is most swiftly spread through the lungs into the heart—the primary organ of life—and into the arteries, until it finally creeps throughout the entire body. It first corrupts the spirits <note>the "vital spirits" thought to carry life through the body</note>, then the humors, and lastly the very substance of the limbs. 

<margin>Hippocrates, *On the Nature of Man*.</margin>
Diseases, as Hippocrates testifies, that proceed from the strongest parts of the body are the most severe; and if they persist where they began, it is inevitable that when the strongest part is suffering, the entire body will be affected. In the meantime, one must remember that from a long-festering rot <note>original: "putredine"; the historical concept of the "putrefaction" of bodily fluids</note> or some other more hidden cause, a poison <note>original: "uirus"; here used in the classical sense of a potent toxin or venom</note> can even arise and be generated within ourselves.

<margin>Book 6 of *On the Affected Parts*.</margin>
Galen teaches that the ancients debated this question, concluding with the clearest reasoning that the same symptoms are produced both by drinking a lethal poison and by a corruption that can spring forth from within the body itself.

Thus, in the *Life of Mark Antony*, **Plutarch** reports on this same matter: that Antony's mind, bound by magical incantations and amatory drinks, lost its own freedom and remained fixed upon **Cleopatra’s** face—desiring more to return to her than to achieve victory.

<margin>
Poisoning of livestock.

<margin>
Plagues of living creatures.

Furthermore, no one denies that beasts of burden are sometimes fatally afflicted when a poison is administered to them, or placed in such a way that it harms them through its vapors <note>original: "halitu"; refers to poisonous mists or exhaled breath</note>. However, it has been recorded by the best writers on agriculture, the veterinary arts, and "mule-medicine" <note>original: "mulomedicinæ"; a specific branch of ancient medicine focusing on beasts of burden</note>—both ancient and modern—that these animals are more often struck down in great numbers, even to total extinction, by severe plagues peculiar to them which do not infect humans. Likewise, they are suddenly carried off by other rapid diseases specific to their species; some of these are also common to humans, while others are unique to livestock. Yet these diseases are frequently believed to be the result of witchcraft <term>maleficia</term> by people of common intellect, to say nothing of others.

We observe this often, and we remember it happening in years past, that a certain pestilence might slaughter only oxen. Other diseases creep in that kill pigs, or sheep, or another that carries off chickens. **Virgil** beautifully describes a plague that carries off both livestock and wild beasts:

<margin>3rd book of the *Georgics*.</margin>

> From the tainted air a piteous season once arose
> and burned with the full heat of autumn;
> It consigned every race of livestock and wild beast to death,
> It fouled the lakes and tainted the fodder with corruption <note>original: "tabo"; refers to a foul or poisonous fluid/decay</note>.

### Book Three

...its seed. But to those who repent, this promise of abundance is made in Joel 2: "The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people, and says: Behold, I will send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them. And I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations." <note>original: "Zelatus est Dominus terram suam, & pepercit populo suo..." quoting Joel 2:18-19.</note>

However, some people, enduring this loss of their property with impatience, do not accept it as coming from God as Job did; instead, they flock to diviners, soothsayers, sacrificers, and patrons of diabolical actions. ### Book Four.

These magicians claim for themselves a hereditary right to this prerogative of an art passed down, as it were, from hand to hand. They do so because the Egyptian priests—from whom Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato learned magic—used to record the remedy by which each person had been restored to health. These records were deposited in Memphis, within the Hephaesteum <note>The Hephaesteum was the temple of Ptah in Memphis; the Greeks identified the Egyptian god Ptah with Hephaestus (Vulcan).</note>, the sanctuary of Vulcan and Isis. In the same manner, the Greek priests, who were the presiding officers of magic, kept their own observations stored in the inner sanctums of the temples of Apollo and Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine; his temples, called Asclepeions, served as early hospitals where "divine" cures were recorded.</note> in Pergamum. The priests, as if instructed by the oracle of Asclepius, would share these observations with the sick, by whom they were usually accepted with the greatest confidence.

<margin>Galen, Book 5, *On the Composition of Medicines according to Kind*; and Book 6, *Epidemics*. Herodotus, Book 1.</margin>

There exists a sacred opinion against the impudence of these men, written by the distinguished Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) is often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>. Although he was a pagan by religion, he refutes these men not only sharply but also piously, accusing them of impiety:

<margin>*On the Sacred Disease*.</margin>

> "Those," he says, "who boast that they can drive away the afflictions of diseases through purifications and magic incantations, are men lacking a livelihood. They attribute their words to a **demon** <term>demon: in this classical context, a supernatural being or spirit, not necessarily purely evil, though the author views them as diabolical</term> so that they may show off to the common people that they know something more, and thus they deceive men. For they perform expiations for those seized by disease—men defiled by blood and crimes, the unjust and the poisoned—and they bury some of these expiatory objects under the earth; others they cast into the sea; others they carry away to deserted mountains so that no one may touch them. But God," he says, "who purges the greatest and most wicked sins, is our liberation."

[Eucha]rist <note>original: *ristiæ*; the end of the word *Eucharistiæ*</note> they unhappily dare to celebrate. Master **Johannes** Nider <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438) was a German Dominican theologian whose work *Formicarius* and *Preceptorium* were early influential texts on the nature of witchcraft.</note> shows this in his *Preceptorium* <note>A commentary on the Ten Commandments.</note>, saying:
> Sorcerers <term>malefici: individuals who use magic to cause harm</term> want the instruments of their malice to be touched by the sacraments of the Church or by other divine things: such as by drawing a thread through the holy chrism <note>A consecrated oil used in baptism and other rituals.</note>, placing an earthen image under the altar stone <note>original: *pala altaris*</note> for a time, and doing similar things. But these things happen by the instinct of the demon for a three-fold reason, as the same doctor recounts. First, so that not only may men become faithless on such an occasion, but also sacrilegious, by contaminating divine things as much as lies in them, so that they may more greatly offend their Creator, and more deeply contaminate their own souls, and cause more people to fall into sin. Second, so that God, being gravely offended by men—according to the opinion of the blessed Augustine—may grant the demon greater power over evil men; to whom God, in His anger, grants what He would deny in His mercy. Third, so that under the appearance of a seeming good, they may more easily deceive many simple people, who—having touched divine things and used prayers—think they have obtained some divine power from God, where in fact only more serious sins had been committed. These are his words.

In other superstitions, however, which are practiced by these rural folk, even if demons are not explicitly invoked, they nevertheless interpose themselves in these acts and superstitions so that the minds of men may be deceived. Thus far that theologian. And in Question 2, Section 8: "Bishops are held captive by the devil, who, having abandoned..."

Theologians prove that such people renounce the faith, drawing from **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity whose writings on magic and superstition were authoritative in the 16th century</note> in the 27th Case, 7th Question, under the heading *You shall not observe* <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard collection of Canon Law used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>. As a pagan, an apostate, and an enemy of God, he heavily incurs the wrath of God for eternity, unless, corrected by ecclesiastical penance, he is reconciled to God.

<margin>
The detestable abuse of Sacred Scripture and the names of God.
</margin>

To this end—so that piety <note>original Greek: *εὐσέβεια* (eusebeia); meaning reverence or godliness</note> disguised in its own false colors might win over the hearts of many, and by a borrowed charm <term>lenocinio: literally the trade of a pimp; here used to mean a seductive or deceptive enticement</term> cautiously lure others into loving it—the pure words of Sacred Scripture, whether used alone or mixed into a ritual, as well as the names of God, are twisted to their purpose, whether they like it or not. But how appropriately this is done, let those judge who more deeply understand the mystical word of God, His essence, and His living power. 

We must, however, admit that this abuse of the word of God is utterly detestable, and this profanation of the most holy name of God must rightly be called a horrible crime. Truly, no lie is more brazen or more insulting to God than the claim that a new effective power <note>original: *vim effectricem*; the magical belief that certain words possess an inherent power to force physical changes in reality</note> leaps out from a recited verse of Scripture or a spoken name of God to achieve our goals—whether in matters of play, serious business, or as a remedy against diseases—in a way that contradicts the order God established for Scripture and the use of His most holy name. Of what kind [are] these most holy...

<header>Book Four.</header>

...having <note>Continuing the description of the figure from the previous page.</note>, with a bowed head, bald, ascending and descending in the neck of the flask, no differently than specks of dust <note>original: "atomi." Cardano is comparing the movement to motes of dust dancing in a sunbeam.</note> usually do in sunlight. Moreover, he was seen for nearly an eighth part of an hour. They report that the person who stole them suffers some affliction while these rituals are performed, provided they are done correctly. While he was telling these things, a desire to test such matters took hold of me, and an opportunity presented itself.

A certain woman of the household, seized by a desire to see certain things, called another woman quite skilled in such matters. They prepared the <term>ritual sacrifice<gloss>original: "sacrificium." In this context, it refers to the ceremonial preparation and offerings used to induce a vision, rather than a blood sacrifice.</gloss></term>. Three girls (as they themselves reported) saw many things; I was away at that time. Later, I called the woman back myself, and the ritual was prepared: olive leaves were not present, there was no <term>Lord’s Prayer<gloss>original: "precatio Dominica."</gloss></term>, no <term>Angelic Salutation<gloss>original: "salutatio Angelica," the Hail Mary.</gloss></term>, but only a small tent, enclosed on all sides, was added <note>Scryers often used small tents or coverings to control light and focus the gaze on the reflective surface.</note>. The woman herself was present, and she was not the only one who saw things, for the girls did as well: not in the neck of the flask, but in that cone which stands at its base; not in the water, but in the glass; not as complete images, but as if only the upper part; not large effigies, but no smaller than the nail of one's little finger; not descending from the upper part, but ascending from the bottom as if from the empty space of the cone.

The girls reported that they saw these things, as did that boy of whom I spoke before, who also claimed he saw his brother then living in Spain <note>original: "Hispanijs."</note>, while the girls saw other relatives of theirs: a marvelous thing, or perhaps just a fable. <margin>The genuine use of the Word of God.</margin>
JESUS brought forth and proclaimed for the sake of wretched and lost men, so that—since they were separated from God by the fall of our first parents and had lost all grace—they might learn from this that they have been restored to favor. Since the brain remains unharmed, no part of its life is lost. Furthermore, the common folk, ignorant of such things, believe that this power resides in the words. <margin>Giovanni Francesco Pico <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), a philosopher who wrote extensively against magic and astrology.</note> discusses this at length against Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindum" — Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD) was an Arab philosopher who theorized that everything in the universe emits "rays" and that words could project these rays to cause physical effects.</note> in Book 7, Chapter 6 of his work *On Superstitious Foreknowledge against Magic*.</margin>

Furthermore, it surpasses all stupidity that many claim certain voices correspond with certain images of the sky <note>This refers to astrological "images" or constellations.</note>, and that certain words uttered with solemnity can change the senses of humans and beasts. From this, they say, images are seen in a consecrated mirror; from this, women are moved to love; from this, the elements are changed, the earth is variously affected, fire ceases its burning, and diseases are cured. Oh, incomparable madness! What is this power, I ask? From where is it derived, and where is it received? For if the entire power <note>original: "uirtus"</note> of words depends on celestial harmony, as Al-Kindi contends, why can that harmony not operate through itself, since it is the superior cause?

Perhaps he will say that the sky acts through words as a mediate and proximate cause. But let him teach this: is the power of operating received in the sound, or in the voice, or in the external words? For sound is prior in nature to voice, and voice is prior to words: for words are made from voice, and voice is made from sound, since words include voice and sound, and the definition of voice contains sound. There can be sound without voice, because it is prior in nature; for the same reason, there can be voice without words. But without voice and sound, there are no words.

If, therefore, the power is received in the sound, and as sound it moves the elements, then that virtue could be communicated to every sound of even inanimate bodies; therefore, neither voice nor words would be needed. If, however, the power is in the voice—since that belongs to most living creatures besides humans—the same could be done even by brute beasts. But if you say it is received only in human words, I ask from where is the power received? In the first syllable, or the middle ones, or the last? If it is in the syllable, then it is no longer in the words; and that syllable soon perishes. The same logic will apply to the others. Where-

It was God who, from the beginning, instilled marvelous and peculiar powers into specific things to produce the effects of certain actions. For in these man-made objects, no new mixture of qualities is established, nor is a new and essential form poured into a material that was already clothed in a suitable temperament of qualities by the primary ordination of nature. Rather, the material and the form by which the body exists are preserved as they were previously shaped; and when it is adorned by its own natural temperament, art merely attaches a new appearance <note>original: "species," here referring to the outward shape or "accidental" form given by a craftsman</note> to it. To this appearance, the stars contribute nothing, nor do the qualities existing in the air at that time.

# On the Deceptions of Demons

<margin>
From the *Book on Superstitions*.
</margin>
...things made by human art do not derive their power from their material or their form. He [the author] feels the same way about spoken words: words change nothing unless they are heard. Therefore, the theologian Martin de Arles <note>Martin de Arles (d. 1544) was a Spanish theologian who wrote extensively against popular superstitions and witchcraft</note> most correctly writes that it is an error to believe that images made of bronze, lead, gold, white or red wax, or any other material—whether they are "baptized," adjured, or consecrated (or rather, cursed) through the arts of magi and on certain days—obtain the "miraculous virtues" described in the books of such arts.

<margin>
Thomas Aquinas in *Against the Gentiles*, *On Fate*, *On the Occult Works of Nature*, and especially in the second part of the *Summa Theologica*.
</margin>
Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> also proves, using the testimony of Augustine in the tenth book of *The City of God*, that the philosopher Porphyry’s <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist who explored the relationship between physical objects and spiritual entities</note> opinion on constructing such images was false. It is indeed true that natural things derive their forms and powers from the celestial bodies <note>the stars and planets</note>; however, artificial images <term>artificiales: objects crafted by human skill rather than occurring naturally</term> can absorb no power from the artist’s craft, nor gain any force other than what they already possess by nature of their material. Shape <note>original: "Figura"</note> is not a principle that causes physical change. Therefore, gold in the shape of a specific image has no more cause for power than gold in any other shape. But if it appears that some effect is achieved, it happens through the operation of demons playing tricks on humans, according to Augustine. 

Thus, these "astronomical images" <note>talismans intended to capture planetary influences</note> gain their force through a demon. The proof of this is that certain characters <term>characteres: magical signs, sigils, or symbols believed to hold power</term> must be engraved upon those images, even though such marks have no natural power to perform any action. Nevertheless, astrological images differ from magical idols in this: in the composition of magical objects, there are explicit invocations of demons. Consequently, those types of effigies belong to express pacts <term>pacta: formal agreements or contracts between a human and a demon</term> with demons.

They will say, however, that there are forms in the Ninth Sphere <note>In traditional geocentric cosmology, the Ninth Sphere or "Primum Mobile" was the outermost moving sphere that governed the motion of the stars</note> which are seen in India. Indeed, that wicked man from Abano <note>Pietro d’Abano (c. 1250–1316) was an Italian physician and astrologer often accused of heresy and magic</note> fabricated this idea. But even if it were granted: who later taught that *this* character belongs to the Sun, and *that* one to Saturn? From this it is clearly evident that these were the pure inventions of men mocking others. Many more ravings of the magi from Artephius are recited in that same place in order.

If the magi contend that they use natural things—characters, figures, herbs, and words—while otherwise professing to loathe public dealings with demons, they are refuted on this point: for it is a fact most well-established among Aristotle and all natural philosophers that active powers <note>original: "actiuas uirtutes"</note> cannot reside in figures, or letters, or any characters whatsoever. This is because they are nothing other than a composition and order devised by an artist, whether painting or sculpting them. Furthermore, it is a most attested fact that material images cannot work beyond their own species and form, much less produce miraculous effects above the laws of nature. If they are said to be signs, since they were not divinely instituted—but rather rejected and abhorrent to nature—it remains that they are more than superstitious; they are invented by a demon, either by crafting them openly or by secretly suggesting them to the imagination of those of poor faith. It is likewise a dream that Al-Kindi the Arab <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873) was a philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age; his influential work *On Rays* argued that everything in the universe, including spoken words and written symbols, emits physical rays that can influence the world</note> imagines: that figures and characters impressed in elemental matter emit rays by which motions are excited in other things. Since these are made by human art, they in no way move the influence of higher causes. To these, add the ravings of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul, demons, and the use of rituals to purify the mind</note>, by which...

<margin>The power of steadfast credulity.</margin>
Now, the extent to which steadfast **credulity** <note>original: *credulitas* — here used to mean a blind, uncritical, or "rash" belief that lacks the divine foundation of true faith</note> prevails is well known among the common people. Superstition requires credulity, just as true religion requires faith. Indeed, a hardened credulity can do so much that it is believed to work miracles even in false opinions and actions. For anyone in their own religion—even a false one—so long as they most firmly believe it to be true, raises their own spirit by that very principle of credulity until it is likened to those spirits who are the leaders and princes of that religion; and thus, they seem to perform things that nature and reason do not discern. Conversely, hesitation and distrust weaken the intended work, not only in superstition but even in true religion, and they sap the sought-after effect, even if it has been confirmed by much use.

<margin>From *On Occult Philosophy*, book 1.</margin>

Truly, because those ancient **Magi** <note>original: *magi* — here referring to practitioners of ritual magic rather than the biblical Three Kings</note>, and those who stood as the authors of that art among the ancients, were Chaldeans, Egyptians, Assyrians, Persians, and Arabs—whose religion was entirely perverse and defiled by the worship of idols—we must take the greatest care not to allow their errors to dominate the pure truth of our Christian religion. For this would be blasphemous, and an **abomination** <note>original: "βδέλυγμα" (*bdelygma*) — a Greek term often used in the Bible to denote something loathsome, particularly an idol or a ritual pollution</note>. # Book Four

I heard the following story from a clergyman, a theologian of no small reputation. He recounted that a certain scoundrel happened to visit a poor woman who had been suffering for some time from a chronic inflammation of the eyes <note>original: *lippitudo* — a medical term for bleary, weeping, or inflamed eyes</note>. This man promised a most certain cure for her eyes and hung a little scroll <note>original: *schedula* — a small slip of paper or parchment used as an amulet</note> around her neck. He strictly cautioned her that she must not remove, open, or read it, asserting that she could expect no benefit from it if she violated these instructions in any way. 

The woman, filled with great hope and confidence, even restrained herself from weeping—which previously had worsened her eye condition—and in this way, she gradually recovered. Eventually, because she had regained her health, the scroll was handled carelessly and fell off. Noticing the loss of the item in which she had placed her sole trust, her tears returned and the affliction broke out again. Meanwhile, the scroll was found by someone else, opened, and read. Written in the German language, it said these words:

<margin>A ridiculous scroll hung around the neck.</margin>

*May the devil scratch your eyes out and shit in the holes.* <note>original German: "Der teuffel kratzē dir die augen auß, und scheisse dir in die löcher."</note> If translated word for word, it means: *The Devil shall pluck out your eyes and fill their sockets with his dung.* If there had been any inherent power in these words, her eyes would have been torn out and perished, with the cavities filled back up by the demon's excrement.

<margin>Book 28, chapter 7.</margin>
According to a report by **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*, a massive Roman encyclopedia often cited by Weyer for its mix of science and folklore</note>, it seems not altogether different for warding off eye inflammation if a paper inscribed with two Greek letters, **P** and **A** <note>Rho and Alpha</note>, is tied with a linen thread and fastened around the neck.

<margin>A useless slip of paper tied around the neck.</margin>
Similarly, for a certain girl who was occasionally agitated with terrifying madness by a demon, a man of the clerical profession hung a little paper <note>original: *chartula*</note> covered in leather around her neck—which he claimed had been previously consecrated during the recitation of the **Mass** <note>The central act of worship in the Catholic Church; Weyer is skeptical of using sacred rites to "charge" physical objects with power</note> at the altar.

He compares this to ancient superstitions found in Pliny and contemporary clerical abuses of religious objects.</summary>

...even without distrust, the power of the active mind will nevertheless perform its work. This can be clearly seen in toothaches, for which this sort of treatment is most frequent. For the enchanter <term>præcantator</term> <note>One who recites charms or incantations over a patient.</note> moves the mind of the non-resisting patient in such a way that, while he mutters his charms or works with magical signs <term>characteribus</term> <note>Written symbols or talismans believed to hold occult power.</note>, the pain is gradually extinguished. Here I will interject that I remember the toothache of a certain noble girl being eased by a noble man. Truly, he who approaches the act of chanting without faith and persuasion will waste his effort—unless by chance he finds a mind so stupid that it does not realize it is being deceived by the pretense. Therefore, it is not the incantations <term>carmina</term>, nor the magical signs, which are capable of such things; it is the power of a confident mind, acting in harmony with the patient. Things that purify demons.
</margin>
In this kind of religious practice, it was believed that sulfur had its own place in driving away evil demons through fumigation. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on magic and "theurgy."</note> writes that priests used to employ this in purifications, just as they did with bitumen <note>original: "asphalto"</note> or washing with sea water. He notes that sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, while sea water does so because of its "fiery" portion. <note>Ancient science often associated the saltiness of the sea with the element of fire.</note> The herb cinquefoil <term>pentaphyllon</term> <note>Literally "five-leaf" in Greek; often used in medieval charms.</note> is also thought to purify; therefore, ancient priests used it for this purpose, just as they did olive branches. The olive is said to be of such great purity that they say an olive tree planted by a harlot will either remain forever fruitless or wither away entirely.

Things believed to remove the evil eye and sorcery.

In a similar way, people believe that incense, myrrh, vervain, valerian (called *phu* by the Arabs), the castor oil plant <term>palma Christi</term> <note>Literally "the Palm of Christ," used here as a protective amulet.</note> when carried, or dried bryony root, and the fumigation of dried birthwort <term>aristolochia</term> root contribute to purification. This also includes the "blessed herb," the clove-scented herb <term>gariophyllata</term> <note>Likely wood avens (*Geum urbanum*), a common herb in folk medicine.</note>, and sea squill <note>original: "scilla"</note> hung upon the threshold of the house. Similarly, the fumigation of the gall of a black dog, or its blood smeared across all the walls, is said to be especially effective both for expelling evil demons and for removing sorcery <term>maleficia</term> <note>Acts of harmful magic or witchcraft.</note> wherever it may be. There are also other things recommended by the ancients against the evil eye <term>fascinationes</term>, such as a piece of palm wood filed with a bone tooth, or the root of the "satyrion" orchid, specifically the female variety, which is distinguished by the spacing of its joints and its bushier growth.

...roaring with a shout into the clouds) they fly to the noisy cymbals, which are called bells, trusting more in those bellowings—which are empty before God—than in prayers and fasts. Olaus Magnus the Goth <margin>Book 3, chapter 8, *On the Northern Peoples*.</margin> writes something similar about his fellow countrymen: that when the crashing sound is stirred up in the clouds, they shoot arrows from bows into the air, showing that they wish to bring aid to their gods, whom they then believe are being attacked by others. They used these so that through them, as if by "Claudian thunder" <note>original: *Claudiana tonitrua*. This refers to ancient theatrical devices, such as stones rolled in bronze vessels, used to mimic the sound of thunder on stage.</note> and through the customary imitation of things, they might express the crashes of heaven, which they believed were provoked by hammers. By imitating the force of such a sound in the manner of a blacksmith, they considered it quite a religious act to be present at the wars of their gods in this way. This use of "Hammers of Jupiter" <note>These are likely the hammers of Thor, whom the author identifies with the Roman god Jupiter/Jove.</note> lasted until the year 1130 after the birth of Christ.

Among our own ancestors as well, due to the unhealthy teaching of their pastors, a conviction grew over a long series of years: that mugwort <term>artemisia</term> <note>A common plant often associated with protection and herbal medicine.</note> hung before houses during the festivals sacred to Saint John the Baptist, as well as other shrubs and plants—and even candles and torches sprinkled with holy water <term>aqua lustralis</term> <note>Water used for ceremonial purification.</note> or somehow consecrated on certain more famous designated days—[are effective] when the need arises against storms, lightning, and thunder. Ancient testimonies and examples of this matter are found in great number and are irrefutable in the holy books of truth <note>The author refers here to the Bible, specifically the Gospel accounts cited in the margin where Jesus and the apostles cast out demons through faith and the Word rather than physical objects.</note>.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> boasts that he, in the presence of Emperor Vespasian, saw a certain man of the Hebrew nation named Eleazar apply a ring to the nostrils of one possessed by a demon—beneath the seal of which was a root discovered by Solomon—and draw the demon out through the nostrils of the man as he smelled it. When the man suddenly fell to the ground, Eleazar banished the demon with a song of incantation attributed to Solomon. Here it must certainly be admitted that Josephus the Jew, as well as Vespasian the pagan and Eleazar the Hebrew, were deceived by the illusions of the devil. The devil pretended to be drawn out by the power of the root ascribed to Solomon; he did not leave by compulsion, but voluntarily, with God's permission. For he feigns being forced so that he may more cautiously drive others mad, and so that more faith might be placed in the ring or the fictional root—material objects entirely unfit for driving out a demon. This is done so that people do not flee to God, the only legitimate expeller of Satan, in the proper order. And so that the conclusion of the fable might be finished with a falsehood consistent with its beginnings, this act—impious in itself—was covered with a respectable cloak so that the trickery would not be questioned, and so that the art ascribed to Solomon might gain weight and reputation...
