# On the Delusions of Demons

Rash and insolent little men, clergy by profession but in the filth of their lives far too worldly (the very sort of actors this drama’s ministry and stage demand), run forward with their prescribed exorcisms and formulas of certain observed ceremonies. They do this to resolve the disease and drive out the demon. Yet, sometimes the demon yields to their curses and oaths—willingly and colluding with them—so that it might strengthen their impiety. 
<margin><note>original: Ἐξορκισταί</note> Exorcists.</margin> 
Should these exorcists not deservedly be counted among the enchanters? Here, so that I may briefly relate some of their observations, from which (as one knows the lion by its claw <note>A Latin idiom, *ex ungue leonem*, meaning to judge the whole of a thing by a small part.</note>) you may measure the rest: 
<margin>Superstitious cure of one afflicted by sorcery.</margin> 
after the confession of the person who will be purified by conjurations, a diligent search is conducted through every corner of the house, in the bedding and mattresses, or under the threshold of the door. They look to see if any material of sorcery <note>The physical objects—charms, herbs, or bones—believed to be the "engine" of the curse.</note> can be found, which is then to be burned. Truly, this practice did not originate from the Apostles or the primitive Church. 
<margin>Abuse of exorcisms.</margin> 
For if someone is completely cured from the devil’s evil act by exorcisms alone, how could those things hidden in corners or buried in the earth be harmful, given they do not touch the body in any way, nor strike it with their vapor? Then, the one harmed by sorcery, on bended knees, holds a blessed candle in his hand; he is also sprinkled with holy water, and his neck is encircled with a <term>stole</term> <note>A long silk band worn by priests around the neck as a symbol of their authority.</note>. Besides prayers, the common Litanies are recited, adding to the invocation of the saints, "Pray for him," or "Pray [ye]," and "Be merciful," "Deliver him, O Lord." And in place of prayers, exorcisms are employed, which are continued at least three times a week; so that by these multiplied intercessions, the grace of health may be obtained. This form...

> Evil spirits fashion certain shadows of honor for themselves, so that they may thus deceive those who follow Christ. He is sent as an evil one by the ruling power. He is permitted when he asks for something: and this, brothers, does not happen except so that the righteous may be tested and the unjust punished. Why then do you fear? Walk in the Lord your God: be certain that what he does not wish you to suffer, you shall not suffer; and that which he has permitted you to suffer is the whip of one correcting you, not the punishment of one condemning you. We are being educated for a heavenly inheritance, and do we disdain to be whipped? Thus says Augustine:

### Book Four.

...as we frequently see happening among those more suited [to such remedies], care should be taken above all that they are separated, and that each one is taken away to her parents or closest relatives by blood or marriage. In this way, each individual can be more conveniently and faithfully instructed and healed in private, with a choice of restoration methods made according to the specific needs of each person. This prevents anyone from attempting to fit everyone with "one shoemaker's last" <term>calopodio; a wooden mold used by cobblers to shape shoes</term>—as is the custom of certain foolish men, liars, impostors, and the presiding priests of superstition and impiety. By using dissolved formulas of prescribed, ill-fitting words, and certain fictitious rites and substances that have nothing to do with the matter, they try to drive out the demon. But the demon only laughs and mocks within the victims, excellently faking a retreat for the most part as if he were compelled, even though he withdraws voluntarily. He does this to involve us more deeply in a labyrinth <note>original: "labyrinth"; a confusing maze of errors</note> of disbelief, should we believe he has been put to flight by these forbidden means.

As for those virgins <note>original: "uirgines"; here referring to cloistered nuns</note> who are more strictly shut away and not permitted to leave, let the sick women offer mutual aid to one another during the intervals between their torments, consoling each other and observing the prescribed manner of care as much as possible.

Two of them still survive, nearly octogenarians, from whom it has often been heard that they would not have wished, even for a great price, to have been without that heavy calamity born from the will of God. When the women received the affliction from His hand and submitted themselves with their whole heart under His mighty arm, entirely denying themselves and embracing humility to such an extent that they even resisted and overcame all their worldly passions—and, in short, conformed their lives with their whole soul to the standard of the divine word—then gradually all those dread horrors vanished.

<margin>What must be done if beasts of burden suffer something unnatural.</margin>
*If indeed beasts of burden* <term>iumenta</term> <note>Draft animals or livestock, such as horses, oxen, and mules.</note> *are believed to suffer anything against nature (which is, however, very difficult to determine, since they often either graze on poisons in the pastures or draw them in by breathing in vapors), first of all, a medicine against poisons or similar ailments can be offered to them, and other things can be administered which we judge will be useful based on natural conjecture and art. This art is learnedly and copiously handed down by* <margin>Columella, On Agriculture, books 6 & 7. Caesar Constantinus, books 17, 18, 19.</margin> Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a late Roman author whose work "Digesta Artis Mulomedicinae" was a major guide for veterinary medicine in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> *in his four books on the veterinary art or horse-medicine; likewise by* Columella, Caesar Constantinus, *and many other ancient and more recent authors. -># ON THE PUNISHMENTS OF MAGICIANS, INFAMOUS witches, and poisoners. Book V.<-

Because my opinion here differs from the common and many-year-old established view, like an appendix attached to the four preceding books: it should not be turned into a fault against me as a physician <term>medicus</term> by profession, as if I were jumping over the fences of my calling. Indeed, since that demonic business is entangled in such inextricable labyrinths <term>labyrinthi</term> that one cannot easily extricate oneself from here, even if one has a sharp-scented Theseus <note>Theseus: In Greek mythology, the hero who navigated the Labyrinth to slay the Minotaur. # On the Deceptions of Demons

He used to carry around a ring in which he believed a demon was bound by exorcisms <note>While we often think of "exorcism" as driving demons out, in historical magic it was also used to "bind" or command them into objects.</note>. He was forced to speak with this demon and consult it about news and other matters at least every five days. He also possessed books regarding evil arts and unholy conjurations, by which means he intended not only to distinguish diseases of humans and beasts caused by witchcraft <term>maleficio</term> <note>harmful magic intended to cause physical illness or damage</note> from natural ones, but also to cure them. 

Therefore, after his term in prison, that man was brought to a public place before the Town Hall <note>original: "ædes Senatorias," the building where the city's senators or councilors met</note> near the market. There, surrounded by a solemn crowd of spectators, he was forced to take a hammer and—according to the formal sentence passed—break open and completely shatter the "prison" of the captive demon: namely, the ring, which had been placed upon a post. In this way, he was to "grant freedom" to his captive—unless, perhaps, you are so foolish as to believe that a demon, who was thought to be constrained by the solid fortification of a ring, could actually be crushed by the violent blow of a hammer. 

It was furthermore ordered that the same man should cast his books into the fire and stand there for as long as it took for them to be consumed by the flames. He was additionally punished with exile after paying the expenses incurred by this legal action. This took place at Arnhem <note>A city in the eastern Netherlands</note> on July 14, in the year 1548.

<margin>
Rings, crystals, glassware, and other objects consecrated to nefarious use are to be solemnly broken. The books of mages are to be publicly burned.
</margin>

For the same reason, crystals, glassware, and other instruments consecrated to nefarious use must be condemned by solemn sentence and publicly shattered. Upon the craftsmen and patrons of these things, punishment shall be inflicted according to the magnitude of the crime, at the discretion of a fair magistrate. Furthermore, what ought to be decided regarding the books of these "curious arts" <term>curiosarum artium</term> <note>a common historical term for the occult or forbidden sciences</note> should not even be called into question; it is a memorable example that all posterity should follow without controversy...

# On the Deceptions of Demons

*...the prefectural staff: Although the bodies of those endowed with honors are usually exempt from torture—except for those crimes specifically identified by the laws—and even though magicians in any part of the world must be considered enemies of the human race; nevertheless, because those who are in our own retinue almost strike at Majesty itself, if any magician, or one accustomed to magical contests—who is called a sorcerer <term>maleficus</term> <note>original: "maleficus"; literally "an evildoer," but in Roman law, this specifically referred to practitioners of harmful magic</note> in common speech—or a soothsayer <term>aruspex</term> <note>one who predicts the future from the entrails of sacrificial animals</note>, or a seer <term>ariolus</term> <note>a general term for a fortune-teller</note>, or indeed an augur <term>augur</term> <note>one who interprets the flight and songs of birds</note> or an astrologer <term>mathematicus</term> <note>original: "mathematicus"; in the Roman era, "mathematicians" were primarily associated with casting horoscopes and forbidden astrology</note>, or one concealing some art of divination by interpreting dreams, or indeed practicing anything similar to these, should be caught in my court or that of the Caesar: let him be stripped of the protection of his rank and not escape the rack and tortures. If, indeed, he is convicted, and resists those exposing his own crime by denying it, let him be handed over to the rack <term>eculeo</term> <note>a wooden frame used to stretch the body</note>, and with iron claws <term>ungulis</term> <note>hooks used to furrow the sides of the accused during interrogation</note> furrowing his sides, let him suffer the punishments worthy of his own deed.*

No one ought to consult a diviner, and everyone ought to cease from divining; anyone doing the contrary is punished. This is according to Salicetus <note>Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, a renowned 14th-century Italian jurist</note>.

No one ought to consult an enchanter about things to come, nor Chaldeans <note>a term historically used to refer to Babylonian astrologers and magicians</note>, nor sorcerers; and whoever does so shall be subject to the capital punishment of the avenging sword. According to Vivianus <note>Vivianus Tuscus, a 13th-century legal commentator</note>.

Those who invoke demons, or enchant wax images <note>original: "imagines cereas"; figures used in sympathetic magic, often melted or pierced to harm a victim</note>, are punished. This is according to Salicetus.

Those performing incantations for an evil purpose are to be punished; according to Canon Law <note>the body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership</note>, this applies even if they do so for a good purpose <note>the original text notes that the Church forbids "white magic" or healing spells just as strictly as "black magic"</note>.

### On the Illusions of Demons

...[she] said: "By some miserable fate of mine, I have until now devoted my efforts to demonic arts, a sinkhole of all vices and a mistress of allurements, leaning only on the hope of your religion, since I despaired of myself. The children carried out their mother's will, but they achieved nothing. # Book Five.

...[the third demon], with no more effort than if it were breaking tow <note>original: "stupa"; the coarse, easily broken fibers of flax or hemp</note>, shattered the chains. <margin>How the Lamiae, deceived by the works of the demon, believe the deeds to be their own.</margin>
Now, because the women called Lamiae <term>Lamiae</term> <note>a term for witches or sorceresses, derived from a Greek mythological child-eating demoness</note> are by sex "little women" <note>original: "mulierculae"; a dismissive diminutive often used in this period to suggest weakness</note>, mostly elderly, melancholic by temperament <term>natura melancholicae</term> <note>referring to the "four humors" theory where an excess of black bile led to depression, hallucinations, and irrationality</note>, weak of mind, easily despairing, and possessing little faith in God: the devil joins himself to them as if they were the perfect instruments. He insinuates himself quite readily so that he may disturb their minds with various illusions. Fascinated by these mockeries, they believe they have actually done the things they imagine, and they even confess to deeds that were entirely foreign to them. Indeed, if you examine the whole matter with a sharper mental focus against the standard of what can be and is done by a demon, and what is believed to be performed by humans through his works and tools: you will find that the demon designed the entire thing, whatever it may be.

I am therefore hardly led to dare to place these women in the rank of heretics. No one deserves that name unless, having been warned once and twice, and yet being imbued with fanatical opinions, they persist constantly and stubbornly <term>pertinacia</term>.

<meta>This page continues Johann Weyer’s argument that women accused of witchcraft (Lamiae) are often suffering from mental illness or demonic delusion rather than actual criminal guilt. ->### On the Deceptions of Demons<-

[...were never done. Because they are] mentally unsettled, provided they have committed no other actual crime against anyone else, they should be examined and more rightly instructed in the principal tenets of our Christian faith. In this way, they may return to the promises they made at the very beginning of their religious lives—when they renounced the devil. Although they later strayed incautiously due to his secret and fraudulent influence (just as we know happened to our first mother, Eve), they may now, having come to their senses, strive with all their might through more wholesome instruction and the grace of God to fulfill those original vows.

In this matter, why should a faithful minister of Jesus Christ have less power through his counter-persuasion than a demon? Such a minister will seek out the sheep lost to the suggestions of Satan <note>original: "satanae"</note> and lead her back to Christ’s fold. 

Indeed, the truth will easily come to light by conducting a careful test during an examination of the Articles of Faith <term>Articuli Fidei</term> <note>the fundamental doctrines of the Christian church, often centered on the Apostles' Creed</note>. If she has happened to wander from the path because she was poorly persuaded, it will become clear. It will also reveal whether she stubbornly resists sounder doctrine after being better taught—thereby deserving the label of "heresy" <note>original: "haereseos"; a formal deviation from established church doctrine</note>—or whether, having been converted and awakened from the lethargy <note>original: "ueterno"; a term implying a deep, unnatural sleep or sluggishness of mind</note> of a corrupted and seduced mind, she sincerely desires and begs from the bottom of her heart to be received again as a member of the Church <note>original: "Ecclesiae"</note> and to have prayers offered on her behalf.

# Book Five.

When a small portion of earth—specifically the kind that priests first scatter three times during a burial, and which has been sanctified by the sacrifice of the Mass <note>original: "Missæ sacrificio," the central liturgical ritual of the Catholic Church</note>—is placed under the threshold of the church by treading it down, it is believed that a witch, if she is inside the temple, cannot then leave. Likewise, take splinters of oak wood from which someone has been hanged or has strangled himself; let these be sprinkled with holy water and placed at the entrance of the church. She will not be able to exit unless you remove the splinters.

<margin>
What must be done in the investigation of a crime committed.
</margin>
However, it was fitting for investigators to observe this rule, which is by no means deceptive: that they should inquire accurately and with judgment into each of those outrages already confessed. They should ask whether the hardships and calamities which the accused say and admit others suffered by their doing are actually so, or exist in the nature of things <note>The author is urging judges to verify if the alleged "magic" caused real, physical harm or if it was an imaginary event.</note>. And if it is found that certain people were indeed harmed, or suffered diseases or loss, such that these designated evils are thought to come from those who have already confessed; then, the means, materials, or instruments by which they were perpetrated should be more deeply investigated. One must ask whether those means, materials, or instruments are fit and suitable for producing effects of that kind. Here, the judgments of celebrated physicians, skilled in the knowledge of natural things and powers, should be summoned for counsel, just as the laws require to be done in other cases regarding them.

<margin>
The confession of one with a damaged mind should not be relied upon.
</margin>

This is done so that a window is not opened to the devil—who has been a murderer from the beginning—through which he might insinuate himself into our legal actions by means of open lies, or by truth fermented with deceit and falsehood. Nor should we give him every opportunity to advance further...

### On the Illusions of Demons

It occurs through the will and secret counsel of God, or the devil is divinely permitted to act; yet the demon often thrusts thoughts into the corrupted brain of a woman as if the deed had been planned by her. ...they examine and understand with reason. In the same way, an infinite number of confession formulas could be reviewed from the public records of magistrates; yet if you weigh them more deeply, you will find <term>αδυνατίαν <note>original Greek: adynatian</note>; impotence or absolute impossibility</term>, or "impossibility" (if one may use the term), inconsistency, vanity, and lies disguised and covered with a veneer of truth. Thus, not long ago, a certain woman held in chains confessed that she had tormented many Vestal virgins <note>Weyer uses this classical Roman term to refer to nuns</note> in a monastery <note>original: "cœnobio"</note> with various tortures of tetanus <note>original: "tetani cruciamentis"; here referring to severe convulsions or rigid fits</note>. Eventually, when she was about to be handed over to the flames by public judgment, she persisted with extreme consistency in this: that while she and her mother had indeed inflicted that calamity upon those sick virgins and she was willing to suffer death for it, she openly confessed that not even the slightest bit of that mixture had ever actually entered their mouths by her hand.

This is the sole aim and machination of the demon, who was a murderer from the beginning <note>a reference to the Gospel of John 8:44</note>: to ensure that as much blood as possible is shed. The matter was indeed carried out just as my father related it. The master, who grieved for him and was well-liked by the prince, obtained permission—despite the judges' reluctance—to keep the man at his house for twenty days, provided he gave a legal guarantee. But little effort was needed; he came to his senses. He became an excellent Christian and persevered until death without any complaint from others—this man whom the atrocity of the judges would have undeservedly afflicted with a cruel execution.

# Book Five

...seemed to be led away, until the peasants, having seized arms, checked that violence and referred the matter to the judgment of the bishop. But I replied: Why do you not rather presume that the evil spirit was with his fellow demons, while the woman was actually with her husband? Why do you devise a real body in a fictitious game, and a phantom in a real bed? What need is there here to multiply miracles to such an extent, and to act not so much as a theologian but as a teller of marvels <term>teratologon</term> <note>original: "τερατόλογον"; one who tells monstrous stories or tall tales</note>, and to choose the harsher side in matters of punishment? ### On the Illusions of Demons

...and that they could be cured <note>original: "curari"; referring to the "witches" who may be suffering from medical melancholia</note>, were it not that they are all poor women who lack the means for such a remedy. This also seems to have been the opinion of Augustine in the 18th book of *The City of God*, chapter 18, where he says: "In truth, no body can be transformed by any art of demons; only the phantastic [element] <note>original: "phantasticum"; the part of the human psyche responsible for imagination and dreams</note>—which is produced through thinking or dreaming across countless types of things—is affected. And since it is not a body, it nevertheless takes the form of bodies when the bodily senses are lulled or suppressed, so that the true bodies lie elsewhere with their senses locked." ...afterward, in whose presence he discerns his error: or even how that error contributes to the progress of the good. ### John Chrysostom, Homily 47 on Matthew, Chapter 13:

> "Do you want us then to go and gather them up?" The Lord, however, forbids it, lest perhaps together with the weeds <note>original: "zizanijs"; referring to the "tares" or darnel in the Parable of the Wheat and the Tares</note> they also pull up the blade of wheat. He said this in order to forbid wars and the shedding of blood. For if heretics were slaughtered, a war would be brought upon the world without a treaty of peace or any truce. 
>
> Therefore, he forbade it for two reasons: one, because it would do no small harm to the wheat; the other, because unless they were healed, they would not escape the ultimate punishments. Therefore, even if you wish them to be punished, and by no means wish to obstruct the wheat, you must wait for the congruous opportunity of time. But what is this, that you will root up the wheat along with them? Certainly it is either because, if you take up arms, he says, it is necessary when you slaughter heretics to kill many of the holy ones at the same time; or because many things changed by the weeds themselves might convert themselves into the condition of wheat. If, therefore, you pull them out prematurely, those stalks of wheat will perish which would have come from the transformed weeds.

<margin>The assemblies of heretics can be dissolved.</margin>
However, he does not forbid the dissolving of the conventicles <note>original: "conciliabula"; unauthorized or private religious gatherings</note> of heretics, the blocking of their mouths, or the cutting off of their freedom of speech:

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological argument concerning the treatment of those who have fallen away from the Christian faith into the practices of witchcraft or demon-worship. It builds on the previous page's theme of showing mercy to the "sick in soul" by applying specific canon laws and the opinions of influential legal and theological authorities like Raymond of Penyafort and the authors of the Malleus Maleficarum.</meta>

<page-num>468</page-num>
<header>On the Illusions of Demons</header>

<margin>Penitent witches avoid physical punishments.</margin>

Note, he says, one very unique thing: there are two types of these apostates <note>An apostate is someone who has totally abandoned their religious faith</note>. One is the type that simply turns back from the faith and follows the worship and obedience of a demon. The other is the type who, after rejecting the faith of Christ and casting it out from their heart, explicitly rebaptizes themselves in the name of the devil and takes on another name. Although both types are condemned, the first type—if they renounce their sin—is admitted to penance and avoids physical punishments, just like other heretics. This is seen in the law regarding the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>A dualistic religious movement often cited in law as the archetype of heresy</note> in the Code on Heretics. Likewise, the theological authors of the <term>Hammer of Witches</term> <note>original: "Mallei [Maleficarum]"; the most famous manual for witch-hunters, published in 1486</note> teach in these words at the beginning of the third part, in question 35:

> If apostates do not wish to turn back from their heart, they shall be handed over to the secular court as unrepentant heretics. But if they do wish to return, they are received just like penitent heretics, according to the chapter "To be abolished," in the section on "the penitent" <note>original: "ad abolendam. §. pœnitenti." This refers to a specific decree in Canon Law regarding the punishment of heresy</note>.

The authority <term>Raymond</term> <note>Raymond of Penyafort (c. 1175–1275), a prominent Dominican friar and canon lawyer</note> agrees in the title on the apostolic see, in the chapter "those returning," where he says:

> Those returning from the treachery of apostasy, since they were heretics, are to be received just like those returning from heresy; and here one term is taken for the other.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If their own confession is urged here again, I dare to respond along with Master Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio of Piacenza <note>Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio (fl. 1520s) was an Italian jurist famous for his skeptical "Treatise on Witches" (Tractatus de Lamiis), where he argued that witchcraft was a delusion</note>, in the tenth volume of his Treatises, *On Witches*: Since such persons are deluded, as has been said, it must therefore be said that their confession is also erroneous and should not be admitted. For a confession must contain what is true and possible: as noted by the glosses of <term>Baldus</term> <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a preeminent authority on civil and canon law</note> and others in the first law on confessions, and by the gloss in the final chapter on confessions in the sixth book of the Decretals, and the law "then Neratius," the final paragraph, in the Lex Aquilia. For a confession is far removed from the act itself (or even the possibility of the act), and whatever is against nature fails in its own principles; therefore it is naturally impossible.

<margin>In criminal cases, one must not rely on confession alone.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, in criminal cases, as a rule, one does not rely solely on the confession of the accused, as stated by Baldus and <term>Angelus</term> <note>Angelus de Ubaldis (1328–1407), the brother of Baldus and also a famous legal scholar</note> in the first law on confessions; I will discuss this further in the second note. <page-num>478</page-num>
<header>On the Delusions of Demons</header>

...and obscure the truth of natural science <term>physicæ</term> <note>Weyer uses "physics" in the classical sense: the study of nature and the physical world</note>, and hide and clothe the wicked arts of the devil, which are abominations <note>original Greek: βδελύγματα (bdelygmata)</note> or detestable things to the Lord God: let us turn away from these, flee them, and curse them, in whatever artful appearance they may be proposed. Let us also resist and cast away their lures and opportunities, which at first glance seem to flatter and please. Nor should we make our bodies—not of our own will—slaves and dwellings of Satan. But rather, let us shut off every entrance for him to attack us, even though he is most cunning and most treacherous <note>original Greek: καὶ πανουργοτάτῳ (kai panourgotatō)</note>, by means of true faith and holiness of life, constantly imploring help from the Son of God with burning prayers. Let us fortify ourselves vigilantly with the living word of God and the help of the Holy Spirit, as if diligently stationed on guard duty <note>original: "excubijs"</note>. In this way, even if that sworn enemy insults us more boldly—though we are enclosed on all sides by this fortification as if by a very strong wall—he may nonetheless not break through or conquer these sturdy defenses.

<margin>
Job 1, 2
Psalm 2
1 Samuel 28
Acts 19
</margin>

Whatever afflictions are imposed upon us, let us endure them bravely and with an even mind like Job, by no means raging against God like the heathens, nor seeking forbidden help like Saul <note>referring to King Saul seeking the medium of Endor in 1 Samuel 28</note>. Nor should we be curious, like the Ephesians <note>referring to the practitioners of magic in Ephesus who burned their scrolls in Acts 19</note>, or wanton, anxiously investigating those things which either do not concern us to know, or are not permitted, or are not beneficial; nor should we inquire from those things which God has strictly forbidden to be sought out. Instead, let us stand firm and cling to those paths which the truth of the Gospel <note>original: "Euangelij"</note> shows us: the furious delusions <term>præstigias</term> <note>The central term of the book, referring to demonic illusions that deceive the senses</note> of the devil and his slippery tri[cks]...

<meta>catchword: way of [the devil's tricks]</meta>

<summary>Weyer exhorts his readers to reject the "abominations" of magic and instead find protection in faith, prayer, and the study of natural science. He uses biblical examples like Job and Saul to contrast righteous endurance with forbidden curiosity.</summary>
<keywords>natural science, Satan, spiritual warfare, Job, King Saul, Ephesians, delusions, faith, Gospel</keywords>

# Book Five
<page-num>479</page-num>
<header>Book Five</header>

<margin>Matthew 25</margin>
...turning aside from the way, lest just as Jannes and Mambres <note>In Jewish and Christian tradition, these are the names given to the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses (see 2 Timothy 3:8)</note> resisted the truth, we too—by kicking back against the command of God—may one day hear that horrifying sentence of Christ along with those who will be on the left hand: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels."

However, I wish nothing to be so firmly asserted here that I would not submit it entirely to the fairer judgment of the universal <term>catholicæ</term> <note>Weyer uses "catholic" in the sense of the "universal" or "whole" Christian church, rather than specifically the Roman Catholic institution</note> church of Christ: being ready to offer a spontaneous retraction <term>palinodia</term> <note>original: "palinodia"; a formal statement retracting a previous opinion or "singing a different song"</note> soon after, if I am convicted of error anywhere.
